en: Now, when there is no specific injunction, there is authority for all sacrifices (1);
and the injunction regarding mantras applies by means of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (2); and that which begins with the latter is the indicator of the end of the former (3).
In the absence of a specific instruction, one should perform the ritual acts with the mantras as prescribed by their single recitation, just like the Udgātṛ;
this applies to all mantras up to those for which no specific rule has been given,
and by the inclusion of the term "beginning," it includes the Ṛg-verses as well.

The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should be a descendant of seers (*ārṣeya*), learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), of virtuous conduct (*sādhucaraṇa*), eloquent (*vāgmin*), neither deficient nor redundant in his limbs, not too dark nor too fair in complexion, and not more than sixty years of age.
The sacrificer (*yājya*) is also described by the first three of these qualities.
When about to appoint the announcer of the *Soma* sacrifice (*somapravāka*), one should say, "Homage to King Soma," and then address him.

When about to perform [the rite], he should respond with the mantra, "Tell me what is great for me. (10) He should not abandon that [intention] even if it has not been spoken; having understood, "I shall do it," [he should proceed]. (11) For the *somapravāka*, he should cause salted food mixed with curd to be brought to his dwelling. (12)
One should dismiss the Prastotṛ and Subrahmaṇya priests before the ritual acts begin.
The sacrificial ground (devayajana) should slope toward the northeast, be covered with grass, and level; furthermore, there should be water to its east.
Regarding this, he said: "It is the *triśukriya*.
In the absence of that, it is a large tree, a well, or a great road;
and there should be no other high ground within its radius.
And [the altar] in front should be the size of a sacrificial ground (devayajana); in rites for malevolent purposes, it should be reversed;
and [the altar] other than that on a raised mound should be the size of a sacrificial ground.
He himself should go for the purchase on the Upavasatha day; or [he may go] toward the north from his house with the mantra, "May the god go to the god.
Having gone a long distance, he leaves behind all evil deeds.
Having approached the path with "The fathers have come," and having stepped upon the northern edge of the altar while looking toward the south, he recites "O fathers, Bhūḥ!
Dhānañjayya says that if there is an interruption in the Yajus formula, one should perform an insertion;
Śāṇḍilya says that one should simply overlook it.
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra:
"Those who intend to honor [the guest] bring forward two mats, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
1. Each of these is recited three times. 2.
He sits upon one of two grass mats for the cow; he washes his feet on the other. He should drink of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) separately with each foot of the Sāvitrī verse.
"This food, this essence, these cows, together with prosperity"—this [formula] is for each [offering] before [the pouring].

"Speech—may it be much; may it be much for me"—this is for the first [offering], after [the pouring]. "Breath is indeed more than speech; may it be much; may it be more and more for me"—this is for the second.
"Mind indeed is everything; may everything be mine"—this is for the third [libation].

(9) All [mantras] end with the word *svāhā*. (10) "Thou art the sap of the forest trees; bestow sap upon me"—with these words he should drink the honey-mixture (*madhumantha*), according to Gautama. (11)
The traditional teaching is that [the term] "vānaspatya" [is used];
likewise for *dadhimantha* and *udamantha*. However, there is a substitution of the flavor [element] in the case of *payasya* and *apayasya*.
Or indeed, in the Vedic tradition, these [names] may be Kālinda or Sārasvata; 15.
one should give the remainder to a Brāhmaṇa; 16.
in his absence, having sprinkled it with water, [one should give it] to a non-Brāhmaṇa. 17.
When the cow has been addressed with "Do it," he should say:
18. "We shall release her; the rite has been performed; let her eat grass and drink water; release her! He should say this. 19.
For all [the officiants], wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta) and the constant sipping of water (ācamana) are obligatory. 20.

There is no interruption or reversal of the sequence of ritual acts by means of the sacrificial subsidiaries (yajñāṅga). 21. And when there is no specific instruction, the preparation of the sacrificial ground is performed facing east. 22.

Once the King Soma has been purchased, the Subrahmaṇya priest, having gone to the north of the Soma-cart, should stand between the two poles holding in his hand a branch of the Śamī tree or a branch of the Palāśa tree with its leaves intact. 23.
In all cases, one should expect the Adhvaryu’s summons; however, in the case of the Subrahmaṇyā,
[one should do so] while holding the reins with a branch, [and] should direct the two oxen,
[placing] the right one first.
One should call out "O Brahmins! Om! three times with a moderate voice while facing east;
six times while facing west.

Having entered the branch into the wife's hall (patnīśālā) once the roof has been removed, one should not step over it nor allow anything to intervene between oneself and it, so that Agni and Soma may be in their proper place.
Thus ends the second section in the first chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
Now, one should give this royal vehicle to the Subrahmaṇya priest, because it is connected with rites that involve sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

When the Ātithyā ceremony has been completed, standing beyond the southern door-post in the area of the inner altar (antarvedi), while the sacrificer and his wife have taken hold [of him], he should utter "Subrahmaṇyo! three times and then recite the formal liturgical address (nigada).

"O Indra, come! O possessor of bay horses, come! O you who were the ram of Medhātithi, the stallion of Vṛṣaṇaśva, the bull of Mena, the one who leaped upon Gaurī, the paramour of Ahalyā, the Kauśika Brahmin who called himself Gautama!
(3) "On such-and-such a day there will be the Soma-pressing"—this [formula] is used according to the specific day on which it occurs.
(4) "Today"—this is used when the day is the same. (5)
One should pause at the end of the *praṇava* in the first two [sections],
and also when saying "mene bruvāṇa" (6).
In the section dedicated to Agni (*āgneyī*), one should pause at "ṣaṇe" and "jāra" (8).

And when there are separate words for the sacrifice, Gautama says that one should say, "O Brahman gods, come, come, come! (9). Hānūmānjayya says that one should say "Come" before the formal invocation of the gods. (10–11)
"Come, O Maghavan!"—thus some say.
Having called out three times in this manner, the *patnī* and the sacrificer, desiring the invitation (*upahava*), being invited, may proceed according to their purpose.
"You are invited"—this is the formula for the invitation.
Thus, in all the Upasad rites,
as well as those following the Upasads;
and standing there upon the Utkara mound.

Before the announcement of the *sutyā*, when the omentum of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma has been offered and the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, at the time of commencing the *prātaranuvāka*,

one should take up each of the sacrificer’s names individually— namely, "So-and-so sacrifices"— as well as the names of his ancestors: "the son of So-and-so," "the grandson of So-and-so," and "the great-grandson of So-and-so."

Then, having stated "of those others, according to seniority, of the women and men who may live" up to the words "of those yet to be born," he should conclude starting from the announcement of the Soma-pressing.
Now, he prescribes the accent for the sentences containing the mention of names: the etymological explanation is uttered with the *udātta* (acute) accent.
In the case of the vibhakta [notes], there would be the vibhakta itself; from high, low; low;
"of those about to be born"—thus two in the middle. 24–26.
The root *yaj* (to sacrifice) begins [the section]. 27.
When being followed while the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) are being urged forward, he should call out the names of those giving the gifts, pronouncing their names. 28.
Or he may utter the names preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ). 29.
Some say that the Subrahmaṇyā call occurs at the moving of the Havirdhāna carts and at the leading forward of Agni and Soma;
the teachers, however, maintain that there is no such call, as the Subrahmaṇyā ends with the Prātaranuvāka.
Thus ends the third section in the first chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.

In the Sādyaska sacrifices, [the offering] is made at the time of the omentum-offering (vapā) in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, or when the two Ājyabhāga offerings have been completed, according to some; however, it is omitted because the locus for its performance has disappeared. In the Agniṣṭut sacrifices, there is an Agneya formula (nigada).
In that regard, according to Gautama:

"O Agni, come hither with the two ruddy steeds, O you of great luster, smoke-bannered, knower of all beings, far-seeing, descendant of Aṅgiras, you who call yourself a Brāhmaṇa of the Aṅgirases"—[this formula is used] prior to the announcement of the Soma-pressing.
At the place of the gods, there are the fires.
Then Dhānañjayya says: "O Agni, come! O Rohitāśva, come! O Son of Bharadvāja, born of Aja Ekapād, you who leap down for our protection, O Dawn-born one!
(7) The portion beginning with "O descendant of Aṅgiras" is the same [as before].
(8) In the unexpressed [verses], he should say "Indra" for Indra and "Viśve" for the gods. (9)
And at the two morning pressings, [the chant] is unexpressed (anirukta). 10.
Between the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya, the announcement by name is always performed. 11.
In multi-day sacrifices (ahargaṇa), one should call out at the beginning and end of each day. 12.

13. [The formula] "for the sake of the subsequent day" is used up to the *ahīna* sacrifices. 14. In the *ahīna* sacrifices beginning with the *agnīṣomīya*, all [formulas] include the mention of the names [of the sacrificers].
15. In *satra*s, the mention of the names of the initiated ones follows the sequence of their initiation.
There is no taking [of the draughts] after the Atirātra;
according to Gautama, the Soma-pressing (sutyā) occurs on the following day at the end of that [Atirātra];
according to some, it is at the end of the Nārmedha.
The first pressing belongs to Śāṇḍilya;
Dhānañjayya says there is no invocation;
and in the last three [pressings], there is the calling by name.

Gautama says [the rule applies] to the two best [cups]. 22. Dhānañjayya says that, such being the case, there is no taking up of the omentum of the Agniṣomīya [animal]. 23. Or rather, there is no announcement. 24.

Śāṇḍilya says that there is no taking [of the draughts] at all throughout the sacrificial sessions (satras). 25. According to the view of Udbhūḥ, there is one [draught] for the Āgneyī [verse] from the Atirātra up to the second Pañcadaśarātra, or two.
26. All [the verses] prior to the Trikadrukas [are used] in the third [Pañcadaśarātra]. 27.

Having understood that for the Kauṇḍapāyina, Tāpaścita, and Citaya sacrifices there is a Soma-pressing on the tenth day, Dhānañjayya maintains that the invitation should be made according to that specific measure. Others maintain that one should invite them for the Soma-pressing [on the day it occurs]. After the Atirātra and before the first Sārasvata [pressing], and prior to the pressing of the following day, Śāṇḍilya maintains that the invitation should be made for both the Kauṇḍapāyina and the Sārasvata sacrifices during their respective sacrificial sessions.
"Thus [is] the Agnihotra month; thus [is] the Agnihotra month" (31). This is the fourth section in the first chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
In all cases where no specific instruction is given, the Prastotṛ should chant the *parisāman* chants according to his own study (*svādhyāya*), using his own [melodies]. 1.
In the *tṛca* verses, one should perform three repetitions; for the others, it is three times.
Or, as in the case of Śārṅga mounted on a chariot, one should practice three times for the descendant of Aṅgiras, with the intermediate [verse] recited in a continuous flow (*parāc*).
And so does the Hotṛ.
And the justification for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is thus [established].
5. In all cases where no specific instruction is given, the path of movement (*saṃcara*) is between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*. 6. The *tīrtha* (the point of entry) is that which leads to it. 7.
While the fire-altar is being built up, he should go behind the tail and stand at the southern armpit, or where they may place [the bricks];
[he should also stand] behind the two wings and the two armpits,
and in front of the two shoulders.

When the lotus-leaf is being laid down, and upon the golden man and the self-perforated pebbles, one should chant the *vyāhṛtis* and the *sāmans*: the *yajamāna-sāman*, the *satya-sāman*, the *puruṣa-sāman*, and the *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar-sāman*, each separately.
In their place, when building by oneself, [one should chant] the *ṛtanidhana*, the *ājyadoha*, the *puruṣavrata*, the *ekānugāna*, the *rathantara*, the *vāmadevya*, and the *bṛhat*.
The *rathantara* and the others are optional alternatives to the repeated *lokasāmans*.
Having gone to the south of the piled fire-altar, standing facing west, he should sing the *Gāyatra* in its explicit form upon the head. 14.
Having returned, he should sing the *Rathantara* on the southern wing, facing north, or behind it, facing east. 15.
Having gone to the west of the tail, he should sing the *Bṛhat* on the northern wing, facing south; or behind it, facing east. 16.
Having returned, the Yajñāyajñīya [chant] is performed on the tail if it is a year-long rite, whether it be the Daikṣa or the Sautya.
The Yajñāyajñīya is placed in the Ṛtu-sthāna elsewhere. The Vāmadevya is in the right armpit.
"The Heart of Prajāpati" is to the north (20).
"O Gautama, having gone to the north of this fire" (21). "Dhānañjayya [says] that one should perform these very [rites] in a clockwise direction from the end" (22).
The Yajñāyajñīya [Sāman] is on the tail (23),
and the Vāmadevya is in the place of Prajāpati’s heart (24).
Having gone to the south of the fire, Śāṇḍilya says that there is an exchange of the two wings according to the Gautamīya [tradition] (25).
Having sung on the head and on the northern wing as prescribed (26),
and having sung the others as they were sung (27),
and having touched his own heart-region on the northern upaplaṣa with the verse "The Heart of Prajāpati" (28).
On the path of the *adhvaryu*, [he sings] "The *śyaita* [sāman]" (26).
Thus ends the first section in the second chapter of the *Drāhyāyaṇa-śrautasūtra*.

Having gone to the north of the *samrāḍ-āsandi* in a sacrifice where the *pravargya* rite is performed, standing behind it and being prompted by the *adhvaryu*, he should sing the *agnāyi* [sāman]. 1.
At every step one should chant the *stobha*;
at the *nidhana* (concluding syllable) one should release the speech of the *staubhī*.
Those who have participated in the *gharma* oblation should approach him as he intones the musical notes beginning with the *upagraha*.
And the wife likewise [is seated] in the middle; having reached the site of the Āhavanīya fire, [he performs the rites].

While the water is being sprinkled, having touched water, [they perform] the Vārṣāhara; when it has been sprinkled, they perform the iṣṭāhotrīya. All of them should join in at its conclusion (nidhana).
If they should carry away the vessels of the *dvīpa* chant, he should continue singing the *santati* chants and not desire the sprinkling of water.
[He should perform] the *śyaita* chant while returning.
The sacrificer should join in at the *nidhana* either on a triplet or on a single verse.

Having entered by the eastern door and gone north of the fires, Dhānañjayya says that one should sing the Vāmadevya, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire while looking toward the place of the Mahāvīra.
Śāṇḍilya says that [the singing] should end with the Śyaita. The subsequent [verses] belong to the Gaṇasāman group.
Some say that these [rites] should be performed because of their beauty; others say one should not perform them;
still others say one may perform them at one's own sacrifice.
Or, according to his desire,
he may sing the two *tārkṣya-sāmans* at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, namely these [two] on the *ṛc*s beginning with "tā amūṣu.
At the *prāyaṇīyā*, he should sing the *pravad-bhārgava*.
At the *udayanīyā* [offering], the *udvat* [sāman];
at the *ātithyā*, the two *gāyatrīsāma* and the *auśana*; there, they anoint the *gharma*, and for that, the *śārṅga*.
They place silver and gold; that is the semen and the moon (26).
He kindles it; that is the two bodies of Dharma (27).
They call it "the pleasing" or "the shining of Dharma," or [the shining] of Indra (28).
They release the cow; that [is] the *dhenu*.

Regarding its deities, one should perform the *stobha* with the *upāya*; one should repeat it without the *upāya* for the [first] three feet, but the last foot should have five *nidhanas*, according to Gautama. One should combine the feet and the deities, according to Śāṇḍilya.
"One should practice the supreme foot again," says Vārṣagaṇya (32).
One should complete the remainder just as it was for the Maruts in the case of the elements (bhūta) (33). They bring milk; that is "milk" (payaḥ) (34).
They pour [the water] with [the verse], "The Sindhu, the Sāmā, and the Indus enter thee";
35 they grasp it with two hooves with [the formula], "These are the two hooves of Vasiṣṭha";
36 while it is being carried away, the two wings of the vow [are used]. 37
When the vow of the Aśvins has been offered, or that of day and night (38), they proceed with the two *rauhiṇa* rice-cakes; that is the *rauhiṇaka* for the Rājanya (39).
They place the vessel for the heated milk (*parigharmya*) upon the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandi*); that is the "as if mounted" (*ārūḍhavat*) *āṅgirasa*, namely the *svar-nidhana* chant (40).
41. They lead forward the fire; therein is the vow of Agni.
42. Agni and Soma; therein is the vow of both.
43. At the Soma-pressing, O charioteer of the sacrifice, [the fire] is placed daily on the Āgnīdhrīya altar prior to the commencement of the Prātaranuvāka.
In the *sattra* sacrifice, there is the prosperity of the *sattra*;
44. if the bull is the animal to be bound at the end, [the offering is] in the *aukṣṇorandhra* [chant]; 45. if it is a bull, [the offering is] the *ārṣabha*. 46.
In the case of *unnata*, [the suffix] *traikakubha* is used;
for *vaśā*, *vāśa*;
and for *aja*, *ājiga*.
The Meṣa [Sāman] is for the Aurṇāyava; 50. the Svāra [Sāman] with the Payonidhana is for the Payasyā; 51.
the Udvaṃśīya is for the Udavasānīyā. 52.
"Having commenced [the rite], one should complete it until the conclusion of the sacrifice" (53).
Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. 1.
When about to erect the sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood, one should go to the east of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), provided that his residence is to the south of it.
If [the post] is from another [tree], it should be to the north.

Having entered through the two pits at the eastern door of the *sadas* between the two openings, and having gone along the front of the *audumbarī* pillar, standing facing north together with the *adhvaryu*, he should raise it with his right and left hands turned upward, saying, "May Dyutāna [raise] thee.
With the words, "Of Āyu," he should place it into the pit.

Having placed [the vessel], he should mutter: "Homage to the ocean, homage to the eye of the ocean; do not carry away my life, O giver of strength! Give me strength, grant me strength; give me food, grant me food.

(5) He should not release them until they have been covered. (6) When the oblation has been offered by the Adhvaryu, he should sacrifice according to that same procedure between the two prongs of the forked stick. (7)
"O Heaven and Earth, you have been gratified with ghee, svāhā!"—with this he offers the first oblation; "To Prajāpati, svāhā!"—with this the second.
Or rather, he may offer only one [of the two], with the word *svāhā* as the second, so that the clarified butter may reach the earth. 8–10.
In the injunctions for the *homa* sacrifice, when no specific substance is prescribed, clarified butter (*ājya*) is used.

Having grasped [the ladle] below the two prongs [of the *sruk*], he should recite: "Make firm the gods in heaven; make firm progeny in me. In the middle [of the prongs], he should recite: "Make firm the birds in the intermediate space; make firm cattle in me. 11–13.
"May I strengthen the plants upon the earth; [may I strengthen] my kinsmen"—with these words, [he offers] at the root (14).
Dhānañjayya says that the portion beginning with the upward oblation belongs to the sacrificer (15).
Gautama and Śāṇḍilya say it belongs to himself; whatever benediction the officiating priest invokes, it belongs to the sacrificer alone (16).
"As it is being covered, [he recites]: 'Thou art a divine covering named Saṃtaninī, the shadow of all people; homage be to thee; do not harm me. 17.
"Having gone to the south of the pits, one should enter between the two other door-posts and perform this," says Śāṇḍilya. 18. "To the north," says Dhānaṃjayya. 19.
The other [rite] belongs to Gautama;
it should be performed in the same manner as he would depart.
Thus ends the third section in the second chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
They should recite the mantra "O manly one, you whose strength is upward" over the sacrificial post as it is being erected.
(1) These same [mantras] should be used in place of the original ones, according to the number [of priests] present.
(2) Śāṇḍilya says they should do so where, while standing, they can see the post being erected. (3)
Dhānañjayya says it should be performed within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi),

because a Yajus formula is not applicable outside the altar. One who has been told by the sacrificer to perform the Viśvarūpa chants in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice should refuse, because of the excess resulting from the completion of the Catuṣṭoma Stomas and because of the absence of the Graha and Śastra recitations.

If one should say, "The *vasatīvarī* waters, the drawing of the cup, the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), and the recitation (*śastra*)—these do not belong to them, nor is there a conflict [of ritual order] as with other *parisāman* chants, because they are sung to the *gāyatrī* [meter]," [the Adhvaryu] should say to the Hotṛ:
"One should not commence the morning litany without addressing me.

Then, having gone by the eastern [door], the sacrificer and the Hotṛ, who is seated for the morning litany, should enter by the eastern door; passing between the two *havirdhāna* carts, the sacrificer should sit silently facing north, in front of the Hotṛ.

To the east, the sacrificer, facing westward, should sing three times the *gāyatra* chant on this verse: "I yoke the hundred-footed speech, which has a thousand paths; the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and the *jagatī*—all forms are gathered together; the gods have made them their dwellings. According to Dhānañjayya, he should sing it in the tone used for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-svara*).
The sacrificer should murmur it mentally alone.
Gautama says that one should sing [the stotra] in groups of three quarters each; 13.
while singing, one should release each preceding [quarter], forming the *gāyatrī* pattern; 14. or rather, one should form the *pragātha* pattern. 15.
Having sung according to the truth (16),

if they are Viśvarūpas, they should also sing the *jyotis* verses (17). When the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been concluded, [the Adhvaryu] says, "The Hotṛ, having approached, shall recite the hymn named Aponaptrīya before that" (18).

Either following the *āgrayaṇa* cup without the *hiṃ*-utterance while holding the filter (19), or having reached the *āstāva* according to the application of the *stoma* (20), one should mentally chant the *gāyatra* melody three times over each of these verses: "Agni is light, light is Agni; Indra is light, light is Indra; Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya. (21)
These [sacrifices] are not other than the Viśvarūpas;
22 the Viśvarūpas are not other than the Jyotiṣṭoma. For these—the Viśvarūpas and the Jyotis-sacrifices—are associated together as "Jyotis" sacrifices. 24
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
Thus the second chapter is completed. 2.
In all simultaneous rites, the Prastotṛ follows the right arm of the Udgātṛ, and the Pratihartṛ follows the left. 1.

When the Hotṛ, having recited the Prātaranuvāka, says, "Uṣas has appeared," then they should step onto the altar with the mantra, "O soft earth, do not harm me. Dhānañjayya says that one should mutter this mantra outside the altar, using only the words "Do not harm me" as the end of the mantra.
And at the beginnings of the pressings, [they should step on it] with a Yajus formula;
Gautama says this should be done day after day.
"At once during the sacrifice," says Śāṇḍilya;
"as long as they can stride [the distance]," say some;
"they should enter after the *vasatīvarī* waters when the *havirdhāna* shed is being entered."

Having touched his forehead, [they say] "The head of Viṣṇu. Entering between the two *iṣe* [posts], having bent down the arms [of the posts] with the words "Food and strength," and lifting up the heels [of the chariot], they should touch the King [Soma] with the words "I yoke [thee]"—this applies to that which is for the morning pressing.
If it is undivided, [it applies to] the whole.
If they do not reach the Soma by way of their respective positions,
the Prastotṛ shall first overstep [the boundary],
then the Udgātṛ, and then the Pratihartṛ.
To the west of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, they should sit down, turning to the left, with the mantra, "The seat of Ṛta.
(14) In all cases, they should mutter the verses both before and after those at which they intend to perform the ritual acts.
(15) But here, [this applies] to the *bahiṣpavamāna*. (16)
When the Soma has been pressed, having touched the *droṇakalaśa* with the formula, "Thou art the vessel of Truth," they should chant the *pra-sthāna* verses with the formula, "O Forest-born One.
(17) The Udgātṛ should hold the fringe of the filter in his right hand. (18) If they should strike against the axle, they should chant the *pra-sthāna* verses again. (19)
Without touching the two axle-props, he should throw the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* into the *droṇakalaśa*;
if both are joined together, [he should do so] from above.
If it is a chariot, he should place everything on top of the seat of the chariot, one above the other, over the lower part of the chariot pole.
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
Having returned, one should yoke the pressing-stones (grāvan),
having placed them clockwise in eight positions, making those that are thicker on the inside.
Those openings—
first the southernmost and then the easternmost—
having touched them, they should mutter the verse beginning with "The Maruts."
Dhānañjayya says that after reciting "O you who sit in the seat of Truth," one should recite only as far as "you are harnessed, carry [the oblation]. 6.
They should place the *droṇakalaśa* behind or to the south with the formula, "Here I [place] this... 7.
In all instances, they should use the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) according to the actual situation. 8.

If the two mantras are performed by another, others may repeat them after him (anujapeyuḥ). This rule applies to all optional rites (*kāmya*) other than those prescribed for Brahmins. However, the rule regarding the "rite for one who is hated" (*dveṣyakalpa*) remains as an exception. Even there, since the inclusion of obligatory duties (*nityadharma*) would otherwise follow, he says: "except for the rite for one who is hated."
Having reversed that [formula],
he should silently perform the joining and the placing;
then, saying "This one, I [place] such-and-such," he should mark out the eighth spot to the south-west.
The king should employ two mantras for those who conceive of him as either hateful or dear; he should direct his subjects toward that [king],
and likewise provide him with food and drink.
The fifth pressing-stone is named *upāṃśusavana*; one who desires to destroy the kingdom should place it above the *droṇakalaśa*, designating a powerful neighboring tribe as his adversary.
Gautama says that having performed one of these [rites], one should perform the *pathyā* rite;
Dhānaṃjayya says that one should perform only that [specific rite].

At the end of the *pṛṣṭha* stotras, having gone out by the eastern door, Śāṇḍilya says that one should cleanse the *droṇakalaśa* according to one's desire; [specifically], with the formula "O Vasus, you... he cleanses the bottom, with "O Rudras, you... the middle, and with "O Ādityas, you... the cavity (21). Dhānañjayya says that one should cleanse it three times at each pressing with each one of these formulas respectively (22–23).
"By all [the bricks] for all [parts]," says Śāṇḍilya (24).
"The bottom by all, the middle by all, and the opening by all," say some (25). "The opening, the middle, and the bottom [by all]," says another (26).
Having shaken out the strainer with its fringes pointing northward, they should spread it downward over the navel with the verse, "The strainer for thee" (AV 6.51.1).
According to some, this is done with the three verses [of that hymn].
While the stream of soma is continuous, the Udgātṛ should mutter, "O bright one, come forward" (AV 6.51.2).
One should designate a beloved king [with the formula]: "For the kingdom of so-and-so";
or "For the kingdom of the king";
or "For the kingdom of the sacrificer-king."

"Either 'for the sovereignty of King Soma' or simply 'of Soma'—one should say [the latter], for Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king. Thus ends the second section in the third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 2.2.34–35.

When the Adhvaryu draws the Āgrayaṇa cup, he utters the sound *hiṃ*; at that time, they should choose [the priests] according to their respective characteristics: "Agni is the Prastotṛ, I am the human one; Bṛhaspati is the Udgātṛ, I am the human one; Vāyu is the Pratihartṛ, I am the human one.
1. Dhānañjayya says: "They should not choose [the priests]. 2. Śāṇḍilya says: "They should indeed choose them. 3.
In this case, they should restrain their speech either at the seat of Ṛta, or while stepping onto the altar.
They should release [the vessels] while the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is being performed.
Carrying the *dhruva*-vessel from the northern *havirdhāna* cart, they should carry it behind the singers and return by that same path;
for even the Adhvaryus may sometimes be unskilled.
Having pressed the strainer, the Adhvaryu should cause the Prastotṛ to continue the chant as it flows out;
the Udgātṛ [should continue] him; the Pratihartṛ [should continue] the Udgātṛ; the Brahman [should continue] him; and the sacrificer [should continue] the Brahman.
"The five officiating priests, holding on to one another, glide along"—thus he says of these.
They should feel aversion because of the mention of defects and because of the exclusion [of the king].

(13) Having touched the king, they should not touch water; likewise, having touched clarified butter, they should touch the king—in all cases, [the sequence is] thus. (14) "This clarified butter is the essence of Soma"—by this, he states the non-conjunction of those two. (15)
When the *adhvaryu* has offered [the oblation], they should offer the *pravṛta*-oblations in the order of their sequence, with the formulas: "Thou art Bekurā by name; may Sūrya protect me.

(16) But if the *soma* has been pressed together (*saṃsuta*), the *udgātṛ* should offer an additional one with the formula: "For reclining, for sitting," while designating the *chandas* according to the respective *savana*.
(17) Everywhere, the third [offering] is made with the verse ending in *svāhā*: "Of the Ṛcs, of the Sāmans... (18)
"Regarding this very point, Śāṇḍilya says:

there is no *saṃsava* (simultaneous sacrifice) when there is an interval of a great mountain, a great river, a chariot's day's journey, or the wind; and also when the inhabited districts are separate."
Some say [the rite is performed] merely by not hating [the Adhvaryu].
(22) Having offered the oblation, they should mutter: "I, the Brahman, take refuge in the Gāyatrī, speech, breath, and Prajāpati; I have surrounded the solid stone.
(23) They should follow the Adhvaryu while crawling along. (24)
With their right hands, they should each cast away blades of grass toward the south, reciting: "He who today, O gentle one... (TS 1.2.3.1).
Having reached the site of the *catvāla* pit, when the Adhvaryu has sat down, they should sit behind him, reciting: "He who is my self... (TS 1.2.3.2).
The Prastotṛ faces west; the Udgātṛ faces north; and the Pratihartṛ, having gone to the west of the Udgātṛ, stands looking toward the southeast, the eighth direction.
Having placed their right [hands] upon the spokes starting from the left, looking at the junction of heaven and earth, and holding their faces level—
thus they should sit for all the stotras.
This is the third section in the third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.

Thus ends the eleventh section in the first chapter. 11. There should be at least four persons as chanters (*upagātṛ*). For thus says the Bhāllavi Brāhmaṇa: "He who takes up a *sāman* that has not been chanted upon (*anupagīta*) is robbed; he becomes harsh and is liable to suffer. He should let it resound for the chanters. The resonance (*svara*) is indeed breath; by means of breath alone he continues the *sāman*. Therefore, the *sāman* should be chanted upon most beautifully. For this reason also, it should be chanted upon. 2.
"There should be four attendants; for the Brāhmaṇa says, 'The four quarters sing along with the directions.
And the Brāhmaṇa says, 'They are the singers. Or as many as may join in the concert."
They should chant along with this syllable "ho," while the sacrificer [chants] "om.
Sitting between the *pṛṣṭha* and *antara* [stotras], they chant softly (*mandra*), concealing the intervals between the musical phrases (*bhakti*).
Except for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the chanting of the *upagītha* occurs at three intervals.
At the morning pressing, however,
they should indeed conclude with the low (mandra) pitch for each nidhana;
even there, they do not stop at every single syllable.
They should speak according to their respective devotion without taking breath; they may take breath either at a word or at a *stobha*, but not between a word or between two *stobhas*.
Or wherever he may be born, he should not let that [debt] remain; thus it is said.
(15) Having taken up the *prastara* grass-bundle, the *prastotṛ* should say, "O Brahman, we shall chant the stotra; O Praśasta! and hand it to the *udgātṛ*.
(16) Having struck his right calf with it, he should join the *stoma* with the formula: "With the splendor of Agni. (17)
Thinking, "I shall prepare the food," he should mutter [the mantra]. 18.
They should silently gaze at the *cātvāla* pit and the water-vessel. 19.
[He should gaze] at the sun with [the mantra], "Thou art the Sāman, shine forth as a reflection! 20.
Or they may chant silently; having uttered the *hiṃ* once, they should chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*. The first *retasyā* verse is without the *hiṃ*, while the subsequent ones are with the *hiṃ*.
The *rathantara* [sāman] is excellent in its syllables and has its *hiṃkāra* unreleased (24).
After its *prastāva*, one should chant four syllables over it (25).
Having praised it with "I have made food," one should mutter [the following] (26).
He should cause the sacrificer to recite "Thou art a falcon" over the *prastara* grass-bundle (27).
Having praised it everywhere, they should all invite it (28).
Looking at the spectators and the assistants, he should mutter the mantra "With splendor... (29).
"Obeisance to the Gandharva"— with these words [he worships] the Āditya;
if [the sun] has disappeared by its mere location,
he should perform all this during the two subsequent Pavamāna chants.
The *pravara* formulas are omitted;
likewise, [the rites] from the looking into the *cātvāla* pit until the *hiṅkāra* are omitted;
and the entering and the sweeping are omitted during the third pressing.

One should cleanse the *kumbha* vessel there; in the northern *havirdhāna*, that which is the eastern [vessel] covered by the *droṇakalaśa* is called the *pūtabhṛt*. It is called the *pūtabhṛt*. 36–38.
Thus ends the fourth section in the third chapter.

Thus ends the first Prapāṭhaka in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. Regarding the application of the Stomas: in place of the formula "May Agni yoke," one should say "May Vāyu yoke" and "May Sūrya yoke" for the two different Savanas.

Dhānañjayya says one should recite "The dwelling through the brilliance of Agni; Bṛhaspati thee" at the morning pressing; "The power through the power of Indra; Bṛhaspati thee" at the midday pressing; and "Through the splendor of Sūrya" at the third pressing.
Śāṇḍilya says one should recite all [the formulas] for each [pressing] according to the traditional text.
At each *sāman*, they should utter the sound *hiṃ*.
During the recitation for the sacrificer, [he says]: "Thou art the bull; thou art the tone.

Having praised with the *bahiṣpavamāna*, he should cut off four finger-breadths from both ends of the *prastara* and throw a blade of grass into the *catvāla* pit, saying: "Whether it be well-praised or whether today it be most excellently praised; whether it be under-sung or over-sung—by one of these two may we ascend to heaven, and by the other may we conquer this world."
Right there, one should pour out a vessel of water with the mantra: "I send you to the ocean; go back to your own source. May we reach you unharmed; do not spill our wealth.
(8) Having gone outside the sacrificial altar, they should step forward with their feet turned toward the north, up to ten steps.
(9) Having turned clockwise, they should proceed to the Āgnīdhrīya shed and recite the verses of the Bahiṣpavamāna chant. (10)

"If someone should say to her, 'He has cursed me,' she should suspect him; against him, she should hurl the thunderbolt of the oblation at the Āgnīdhrīya fire, saying: 'And may the sacrifice be for you, and homage to you! You are the Truth, fashioned by Truth. Whatever of that [sacrifice] was deficient, whatever was left undone, or whatever was redundant, I have perceived—swell with life-breath for that person, svāhā!
(11) One should not deviate from this, says Dhānañjayya.
(12) They should chant the Bahiṣpavamāna hymns in the Sadas hall using the Ahīna formulas, except on the first day. (13)

And in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*) at the beginning and end [of the year], they should complete [the rite] after going out before the drawing of the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), starting from the throwing of the grass-bundle. Gautama maintains that the rule for sacrificial sessions applies to the *Vaidatrirātra*.
Dhānañjayya [holds that] the principle is not lacking.
(17) They should chant softly at the morning pressing. (18) At the two subsequent pressings, they should chant in an increasingly higher pitch. (19)
Or they may eat both [meals] equally at this time; however, in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), they should eat at each pressing (*anusavana*).
Having consumed the portions from the mouth of the *savana*, once the *nārāśamsa* cups have been set down—
thus says Drāhyāyaṇa’s Śrautasūtra, in the first section of the fourth chapter. When the omentum has been offered, they should pay reverence to the *dhiṣṇya* hearths.

At the *cātvāla* pit, however, the first cleansing is performed with this [verse]: "O Waters, carry away whatever is impure and whatever sin, whatever treachery and falsehood, and whatever curse I have uttered. May the Waters protect me from that sin and misfortune on every side; I release myself from it. I release myself from curses, from Varuṇa, and from Yama’s twenty-sixth [sin], and from all evil. May the Waters and the Plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. (2)

Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Thou art the sovereign," they go northward; then, facing north toward the *āstāva*, the *catvāla*, and the *śāmitra* mounds, they worship the sky with the formula, "Thou art well-swept.
With the words, "Thou art pervasive," they should worship the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
To the north of that [fire] is the path for movement everywhere.

When, during the two later pressings, the *havirdhāna* shed and the *āhavanīya* fire are to the south for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* oblations, they stand facing west at the eastern door of the *sadas*. "Vahni" is the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ;
"Śvātra" is that of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
"Thou art Tutha, Uśij, Gandhāri, and Arvāsyu"—with these words, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the others proceed toward the north.
"Be gracious"—with this, they stand right there at the Mārjālīya fire.
"Thou art the abode of Truth"—with this, [they approach] the Audumbarī post.
"The ocean" is the seat of Brahman.
Having gone north of the *sadas* and standing within the altar facing west, they [chant] "The serpent" over the discarded [fire-wood].
"The goat" is the *gārhapatya* fire. 12–14.
"Sagarāḥ" is the location for the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).
"Kavya" is the southern edge of the altar (vedi).
Standing right there, looking toward all [the fires], he recites "pātameti."
"Having approached each one individually, they should say this," says Śāṇḍilya (18). "Making many words into a single unit," says Drāhyāyaṇa (19).
If they should perform the *raurukī* verses, they should first worship the Sun with the verse, "Of paths... (RV 1.50.1).
Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire with that same verse, "Thou art the *apija*, being born... (VS 17.79), or "Thou art the *apija*, newly born" (VS 18.64), they consign Vāyu into the fire.
Intending that [fire], when they reach the *cātvāla* pit and then the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), they say, "Thou art tumultuous; having made thy roar... (VS 18.65).
When [he reaches] the Śāmitra fire, then where they bury the internal organs (ūvadhyam), [he recites]: "Thou art the earth, the receptacle for the internal organs. 4.

When [he reaches] the Āgnīdhra fire, then where the Acchāvāka, sitting down, desires an invitation from the Hotṛ, [the Hotṛ says]: "Thou art the one to be invited, thou art to be honored," or "Thou art the one to be invited, the protector of the body.
5. When [he reaches] the seat of the Brahman, then [he addresses] the Sadasya: "Thou art the Sadasya, the robber. 6.

When [he reaches] the southern edge of the altar, he then [addresses] the wife’s hall with "Thou art belonging to Prajāpati," the *sadas* with "Thou art belonging to Indra," the *havirdhāna* shed with "Thou art belonging to Viṣṇu," the *āgnīdhrīya* shed with "Thou art belonging to Indra and Agni," or alternatively with "Thou art belonging to the Viśvedevas.
Then, in the same manner, [he addresses them] with the entire formula:
"Ye all are worthy of Soma; all drink the Soma; all have obtained the drinking of Soma; protect [us]. The rest is the same.
Having wiped down the two rear door-posts of the *sadas* with the formula, "Stand at the doors of Truth," they should enter with the formula, "May I not be scorched.
Having gone to the south of the *audumbarī* post, they should sit down to its north with the formula, "Homage to my friends.
The *pratihartṛ* should go past the *prastotṛ* on the east.
At this time, in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), all should invite one another; elsewhere,
all should invite the patron (*yajamāna*).
They should perform all this, beginning with the sweeping of the door-posts, when they are about to attend upon the *dhiṣṇya* hearths;

thus says Drāhyāyaṇa in the third section of the fourth chapter of the Śrautasūtra. 16. If the Udgātṛ should perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and the Brahman priest (*brahmatva*), [he should do so]. 1.
Having paid homage to the Āgnīdhrīya fire, he should circumambulate it by the east;
having paid homage to the Sadas, looking from that very spot toward the Pātnīśālā;
the other two [fires] in the opposite manner.
"Ye two are the doors of Ṛta," with these words, having swept the two eastern door-posts of the *sadas*, one should sit down to the east of the southern [post], facing north—thus says Śāṇḍilya (5).
One should sit behind that very [post], facing west—thus says Dhānañjayya (6).
The entry and the sitting have been explained (7).
Having proceeded by the path of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), everything from the general *upasthāna* (salutation) onwards is the same.

However, he should sit down first in the eastern half of the *sadas*. The Prastotṛ sits opposite him. Having cast away a blade of grass to the south with the formula, "Parāvasu is driven out by the sitting of the Brahman," he should sit down with the formula, "I sit in the seat of Āvasu."

"Salutation to the friends who were present in the past; salutation to those who are present now. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! I am Bṛhaspati, the Brahman, a human being. Having said "Om," he should go to the Udumbara post and sit down. (13) The other two should not sit down [at that time]. (14) In this sequence, he should arrange everything according to their respective seats. (15)
If he should become weary, he should stand by the Audumbarī post alone;
in this very same manner, while standing by the Dhiṣṇya hearths, he should enter after the Brahman or the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
Therefore, there should be a joint invitation for him;
the consumption [of the soma] is also common;
and if they should feel repulsion, there should be two separate cups.

While the Sarpas are proceeding, one should not make the assembly hall empty (22). His ritual procedure ends with the consumption of curd (23). He should discontinue [the performance] in the case of Satra sacrifices (24).
When the pressing is disordered, there is a passage between the *hotṛ*’s hearth and the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s hearth by way of the eastern door. "In that manner...
Thus ends the fourth section of the fourth chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*.

Having taken the *camasa* cup, the *prastotṛ* should place it on his right thigh, support it with his right hand, and sit down. (1) While the *iḍā* is being invoked, he should hold [the cup] after [the others], without letting it touch [them]. (2) There is a subsequent drinking for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*; they should all drink in every case. (3)
Having invited one another in secret, the Udgātṛ, being the first,

should place his staff along his right arm, look at it saying "O Falcon," and then, saying "O Moon," he should consume a small portion twice, assigning the meters according to the respective pressing (savana). Then, saying "Upwards," he should touch his principal vital breaths.
"O Soma, take delight!"—with these words [he touches] the heart;
"O Soma, with songs!"—with these words [he touches] the navel. 8.
The other two should do likewise, while the Pratihartṛ stands behind. 9.
He should cause it to swell by touching it while reciting this Gāyatrī verse, "Swell up" (āpyāyasva),
or he may do so with all [the verses].
They should recite that at the third pressing twice.
"May thy milk flow," [he says] at the midday pressing;
Śāṇḍilya says that one should thus cause the pressing to swell by means of a *gāyatrī* verse.
The second *nārāśaṃsa* cups belong to the pressings.
And the third [verses] of the two preceding [groups], 16;

their consumption without looking [at them], 17; [the recitation] with "by the lower ones" at the morning pressing, with "by the Aurvas" at the midday pressing, and with "by the Kāvyas" at the third pressing, 18.
The phrase "by the fathers" (pitṛbhiḥ) should be supplied everywhere [in the subsequent formulas]. 16.
At the touching [of the cups] in return, he may act according to his desire. 20.
He should cause the first and second [cups] to swell at the two preceding pressings. 21.
First, at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana),
having taken blades of grass from the *āvarttis*, the Prastotṛ should hand them over just as he does the *prastara*. He should not omit the mantra when [the blades] are not being brought forward.
In the same way, having struck the calf, he should join the Stoma with the formula: "For consecration, for austerity, for mind, for speech.
(25) According to Dhānaṃjayya, they are separate where there are four [verses] in immediate succession.
(26) Prajāpati is within all of them with the formula: "Thee, O Prajāpati... (27)
By the first [verse], [the rule applies] to those consisting of fewer than twenty-eight; by the second, to those beginning from that number at night;
and likewise, by the third, to those with additional stotras.
Śāṇḍilya says that each [section] should be recited by all [the priests] according to the traditional rule (31).
The principle of repetition applies at the junction (32).
They should not recite [these sections] on the day of the fast (upavasatha) (33).
Thus ends the first section in the fifth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 1.
The Prastotṛ, however, should have mats made from a sacrificial tree; 2. some say they should be from Khadira wood in the case of long-duration sacrifices (Dīrghasattra).

Having had [the sacrificial posts] made one span long, with the backside of *kuśa* grass, unanointed, as thick as the joint of a thumb at the base, and with their tips clearly marked; having smeared them with fragrant herbs and wrapped them in cloth according to the procedure for *kuśa* grass used in *sattra* sacrifices—some say in clarified butter—one should have them stand upon an *udumbara* post, covered by any of the following: linen, hemp, or cotton. On the following day, having wrapped that [post] with *kuśa* grass whose tips point upward, and having likewise wrapped it clockwise from the top down with cloth of that same kind, one should chant the *udgītha* while touching [the post] and not leaning against it; so says Gautama.
This [fire-pan] is a *dhiṣṇya*; one should not place it upon the *dhiṣṇyas*.
Dhānañjayya says that one should lean against it with the formula "Be bold!
For he says: "Thus, being firmly supported, he distributes strength to the creatures."

In the midst of those about to chant praises, having spread out a garment with its fringe toward the east or toward the north, or with its upper part facing upward, the *prastotṛ* should place *kuśa* grass upon it—at the ends of the *prastāva* sections;
in the case of verses with multiple *prastāvas*, at the beginning of each; and in the case of verses without a *prastāva*, at the very beginning.
The first *viṣṭāva* (section) has its tips pointing north; it is oriented either eastward or westward.
(12) To the west of that, [the second] is oriented southward with its tips pointing north, or westward. (13) To the west of that, [the third] is oriented westward with its tips pointing north. (14)
Such successive variations as these, fifteen in number,
he should join together, praising each variation in turn; for at the beginning of each variation, they should chant the *hiṃkāra*.
Having praised the *uttamā* [verse], he should say "eṣā" to the one who is about to recite the *śastra*.
(18) The announcement for the sacrificer is: "Of that which has been praised, you are the praise.
(19) At the conclusion of the pressings (*savana*), having exited by the rear door as directed by the *praśāstṛ*, they should void urine to the west of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed. (20)
They should restrain their speech as long as there are women in their courses;
this is Mṛgatīrtha.
From there, they should proceed further by the distance of a throw of a yoke-pin.

"He who wishes to go further should go by means of reaching [the goal]," thus says the second section of the fifth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. Now, they should worship the hearths (dhiṣṇyas). 1.
Gautama and Śāṇḍilyāyana say that [the rite] is performed with the whole [formula] during both the latter *savana*s; Dhānaṃjayya says it is performed with the whole [rite];
Śāṇḍilya says there is no *upasthāna* (reverential salutation).
In the same way, having stepped out from the individual stotras, they should worship with the collective [sāman] after the ūrdhva-ukthas;
but for the night [ritual], it is after the paryāyas.
Having sat down according to their respective seats, the Prastotṛ should go to the Havirdhāna shed at midday.
The *huta* [offering] occurs during the seizure of the sun; the *pratihāra* occurs at the *ārbhava* [stotra].
(8) In both cases, all [the priests] participate in *sattra* sacrifices.

(9) During the two subsequent *pavamāna* [stotras], while they are carrying [the fire] to the arrangement of the *dhishnya* hearths, they should offer the oblation to the west of the *mārjālīya* and then withdraw by that same path. (10)

Having praised with the Madhyandina [Śastra], they should consume the *dadhigharma* in the sacrificial sessions (*satra*s), having called for mutual permission with the verse, "O Dadhikrāvan... (RV 4.39.6). On the tenth day, they should repeat the last quarter-verse of that [hymn].
They should lead the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) southward by way of the path between the wife's hall (*patnīśālā*) and the *āgnīdhrīya* and *sadas* sheds.
For all [of these], the recitation of "devasya tvā" comes first (14).
One should accept them according to the respective deity with the formula "varuṇas tvā" (15), and for wild animals according to their species (16).
And [the formulas] are without the *prāṇa* [prefixes]. 17.
Duals of the opposite sexes are treated like the masculine, except for those beginning with *ajā*.
18. With that [formula], the recitation "Who has made this? (*ka idam*) follows above. 19.
In that regard, the words beginning with *ūha* (adaptation) are twenty:
"O Goddess, [this] for the giver," and "this [gift] should enter this [person] through that which is on the right," and "may it enjoy this for thee," and "do not harm [him] for a month.
If one should give a horse and a chariot, [these apply]. 21–22.

Having stationed [the horse] to the east of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed and having murmured the preliminary recitation (*purastāj-japa*), he should cleanse the faces of the horses with a handful of *darbha* grass using two horse-names at a time, beginning with "Thou art a horse" (*aśvo 'si*) for each one, proceeding from left to right (*udaksaṃstham*); so says Dhānaṃjayya.
(23) Another view is that the two lead horses (*dhuryau*) are first.
(24) The right-hand one is first, and likewise the two side-horses (*praṣṭī*). (25)
Śāṇḍilya says that all [the formulas] should be recited one by one, proceeding from left to right (pradakṣiṇa).
Another view is that all [the formulas] should be recited in one instance, while the others are recited silently.
One should adapt these very [formulas] as appropriate for horses, mules, and female mules.
If there are three [verses], then half [of them] belong to one [deity] and half to two;
if there are two, they are divided into two parts for each—thus says the third section of the fifth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. 3.26–30.3.

Saying "Of the Ādityas," he should murmur while touching the head of the chariot (1). If it be a chariot for the road, saying "Of Vāyu," he should take hold of the leather covering; saying "Of the Nakṣatras," [he should take hold of] that made of bone; and saying "Of Sūrya," [he should take hold of] the iron and the gold (2).
Having gone to the right side of the chariot, saying "Thou art the Rathantara," he should touch the right wheel (3).
"Thou art the Vāmadevya," [with this he consecrates] the base; "Thou art the Bṛhat," the upper wheel;
"The hooks, the hooks," with these words he should wipe the two wheels.
Saying "Vaiśvānara," he should mount [the chariot] with his right foot.

Having turned back the right wheel—which has already been known and is now fallen—he should gaze at the sky with the [verse], "By the end of the eastern one, O Agnis, thee. The other should say to him, "Thou art mine."
Having climbed up, he should mutter, "May you desire to give" (RV 5.41.19).
10. That too is known: having touched the branch-staff of the chariot of peace while standing between the wheels, he should look along it with this very [verse]. 11.
With the verse beginning "Emaciated" (RV 8.61.17), he should restrain the left reins. 12.
He should cause [the horses] to be given as a fee; he should receive the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā).
Gautama says that having descended, having recited the verse to Varuṇa once, and having assigned [the offerings] according to the respective deities, he should mutter the subsequent prayer.

Dhānañjayya says that having performed all this from the cleansing onwards, and having unyoked [the horses], one should offer separately before and after the prayers with the formulas "To the horses" and "To the chariot," and [recite] the verse to Varuṇa.
If he should grow weary, he should mutter all of this while remaining in his seat (16).
If he should offer the *pṛṣṭhya* chant, he should mutter the names of the horses beginning with those of Varuṇa (17),
or he may do so before the recitation (18).
Likewise, among those who are self-controlled (dāntas),
he should accept from them whatever may be fit for a chariot;
[this applies] to food prior to the offering to Varuṇa and the sheep.
Or, before the recitation [of the *brahman*], [he should offer] twenty-two [oblations].
With the verse, "The *gnās* have cut thee," [he should offer] for the garment; he should cast that away upon a non-woven [cloth].

If gold should arrive in a small amount due to lack of enjoyment, one should fasten it to an Audumbarī post, or one should offer it as an oblation in the Āgnīdhrīya fire. One may accept rice and barley in their entirety at a single sacrifice.
Likewise, one may accept sesame and māṣa beans [as a gift] with the Prājāpatya formula; [one may also accept] things for which no deity is specified with that same formula.
Dhānaṃjayya says that in a non-sacrificial rite, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is offered silently.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," says Gautama (31); or "Oṃ" or "Vauṣaṭ," says Drāhyāyaṇa (32). Thus ends the fourth section in the fifth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. 4.

Having first consumed the *nārāśaṃsa* cup, the *prastotṛ* should offer the *pṛṣṭha-homa* in the *āhavanīya* fire. He should offer the first oblation with the formula: "May that which is the *pṛṣ�ṭha* [chant] designate this; may it drink the Soma-mead; may it bestow unimpaired vigor upon the lord of the sacrifice; may the *hotṛ*s, dwelling together for this sacrifice, be satisfied and well-disposed, Svāhā!
(1) He should offer the second oblation with the *svāhā*-utterance (2).
Dhānaṃjayya says that he should offer the two separately (dvaidham) (3).
"May he drink this Soma-mead; may he bestow unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā!"—with these words [he offers] the first [libation].

"This sacrifice... with these words [he offers] the second. [The offering] for the Hotṛ and the Prṣṭhas is according to the [formula] "for the Hotṛ and the Prṣṭhas. Gautama says that the Vāravantīya [Sāman] is to be applied to the Revatī verses as the designation of the Prṣṭha in the sixth [day].
"The Great Vow" refers to the vow (7);
and Dhānañjayya says it consists of the Revatīs and the Vāravantīya (8). One should observe all those which are the positions of the Pṛṣṭhas (9).
And he should mentally reflect upon the meaning as it is, [reciting] "pibatu dadhat" (let him drink, bestowing).

10. One who is about to chant with the Bṛhat or the Rathantara [Sāmans] should, prior to the application of the Stoma, meditate in his mind on the ten Vyāhṛtis beginning with "airam". 11. In the Rathantara, the verse is "yaste goṣu" (that [milk] of yours which is in the cows). 12.

"Having joined the *stoma*, one should say this," says Śāṇḍilya; "the *ṛc* comes before the *vyāhṛtis*," says Dhānañjaya. In every case, one should close one's eyes while the *rathantara* is being chanted as the *prastāva*.

One should join each individual syllable mentally with simultaneous vocal stobhas, beginning with the letter *bha* and ending with the letter *a*, using the first vowels (*akāras*) that have not been traversed; the last [syllable] is the second vowel (*i*) until the *pratihāra*, having omitted four syllables.
One should observe this everywhere.
Having performed the praise, one should request a boon.
Gautama says that while it is *apṛṣṭha*, the *dharmas* together with the *stobhas* should be omitted.
Dhānañjayya says that only the *stobhas* should follow [the *apṛṣṭha*]. Śāṇḍilya says that one should insert the *stobhas* at the junctions of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* and the *saṃdhi-sāman*.
"The *stotra* should not be chanted with *stobhas* anywhere," says the elder Gautama.

Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. One who is about to chant the *Vāmadevya* [Sāman] should, before the application of the *stoma*, meditate mentally on: "Cows, horses, goats, sheep, rice, and barley."
While reciting the *brahmasāman*, he should attend upon it meditating: "May that desire which belongs to the sacrificer be fulfilled.
Likewise, the other [priests] chant the *udgītha*.

Having chanted with the *ārbhava* hymn, they should enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the rear door, taking one or three morsels from each sacrificial cake, and place them beneath their own goblets when the [sacrifice] has been concluded, saying: "O Fathers, rejoice here; come to drink according to your respective portions."
As it is being brought back, they should respond with the mantra: "The fathers have rejoiced; they have refreshed themselves according to their portions.
When the Soma has been brought back, the Udgātṛ should look at it, saying: "May you bestow life upon me, O breath!
The formula ends with: "May you place [it] back within us."
On the tenth day, one should repeat that [formula]:
"Whatever in my place of intoxication, whatever in my restraint," so say some;
however, one should rather look back at the preceding [formula].

Placing his fingers upon it—some say the thumb and the ring finger—he should wipe his eyes with the mantra, "With that by which [the gods] won the battle. The other two [priests] should do likewise. The Pratihartṛ should stand behind him. They should lead him past the Pratihartṛ to the north.

One who desires wealth should eat this; or one afflicted by disease should go [there], having covered himself with a new garment. Having gone to the southern half of the sacrificial hall (sadas), he should look at the wife at the *hiṃkāra* of the *yajñāyajñīya* chant.
At the *nidhana*, the wife should sprinkle him on her right thigh.
When the third *stotrīyā* has been introduced, he should pour out all that water.
At the final *stotrīyā*, [he should chant] "bhuvadvājāyi" and "bhuvadvājeṣu," and the *nidhana* should be the *anuṣṭubh* ending with the syllable "iti," for it is said, "He says at the end.
However, the teachers maintain that there should be no repetition.

And Śāṇḍilya says that the *nidhana* should be performed according to the traditional injunction. When the Hotṛ recites the *apohiṣṭhīyā* verses as part of the instruction, they should touch him while uncovering themselves. The ritual duties (*dharmas*) belonging to another position should cease once he has reached this [position].
Thus ends the second section in the sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra.
Whatever other *agniṣṭoma-sāman* there may be, its [rules] shall apply:
even when there is no *ahiṃkāra*, at the time of the *pratihāra*, the *udgātṛ* should look at his wife.
They should perform the *anubrāhmaṇa*, the *ārcika*, and the *sannāman* chants everywhere, even in another *sāman*.

At the third pressing, when all the *stotras* have been completed, they should consume the draught and release the *stoma* with the formula, "Of Truth, thee... (RV 10.9.2). With their right hands, they should touch the *kuśa* grass blades together.
Some say that immediately after the sacrificer's speech, at every *yojana*,
or at this point,
he should cause the sacrificer to recite: "For the thread, for me, [be] light."
"May he extend light unto me"—thus [he says] regarding sons yet to be born according to their seniority;
"those yet to be born"—thus regarding those not yet born; and "sons"—thus indeed regarding both those already born and those not yet born in the *satras*.

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered for the *hāriyojana* cup, as they go out by the western door, they should mutter: "O Soma, come hither to me! (12). They should worship the sun with the mantra: "Thou art well-being" (13). If [the sun] has already set, they should worship the *gārhapatya* fire, the moon, or the stars (14).
In the Āgnīdhrīya fire, they should offer two oblations: the first with the formula "Thou art the flower of the waters," and the second with the utterance of *svāhā*.

(15) There are parched grains (*dhānā*) called *hāriyojanī* in the *droṇakalaśa* vessel. Of these, the Udgātṛ, taking the first portion, should say, "We shall eat [them] after having been invited. (16) The other two should do likewise. (17)

Having sought permission from the Unnetṛ with the formula "Hāriyojanasya te... (for thee, belonging to the Hāriyojana cup), they should, at the Atirātra sacrifice—or indeed everywhere—having smelled [the cup] twice according to the recited text, pour it out behind the Āhavanīya fire within the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
[This should be done] while the embers have not yet been removed.
Having touched water, they should throw eight wood-shavings each into the Āhavanīya fire with the formulas beginning with "Of that which was done by the gods... and ending in the dative case.
Śaucivṛkṣi says that all [the cups] should be offered at once with the *uttama* verse. 21.
The cups called *apsuṣoma*, filled with water, are placed in the region of the *cātvāla*. 22.
Green blades of grass are strewn upon them. 23.
Having sat down around their respective goblets, they should touch them with the formula, "Washed in the waters," and mutter [the same].
(24) They should smell their hands with the formula, "Honeyed is the food.
(25) With the formula, "Peace to the waters," they should pour out the goblet toward the north. (26)

Saying "Kāma," they should turn [the hands] inward toward themselves; 27. saying "Ūrj," they should place their hands upon their chests; 28. saying "Prāṇa-soma," they should touch their principal vital breaths. 29.
Having gone to the Āgnīdhrīya shed, they should consume the curd-food without calling for mutual invitation, [reciting] "Of Dadhikrāvan...
(RV 4.39.6). Thus ends the third section in the sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
1. The Agniṣṭapati is the Avabhṛtha-sāman.
Its extension is as follows: 2. All the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should join in the *nidhana* of the first *pravargya-sāman*.
3. Or, they may join in the *iṣṭāhotrīya* at the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, or they may do so collectively. 4.
In the Aśvamedha and Trirātra sacrifices, there are various *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) chants.
Of these, for the first, the *avabhṛtha-sāman* is "sanādagra" (RV 8.42.1).
For the second, it is either "yadvā u viśpatiḥ" (RV 8.43.13) or "tyagnāyī" (RV 8.43.14).

When the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice has been completed, they should touch water and sprinkle themselves three times with the mantra: "O *avabhṛtha*, you are the *nicumpuṇa*; you are the gliding one, the *nicumpuṇa*. I have removed the sin committed against the gods; I have removed the sin committed against mortals by mortals. O you who cry out loudly, keep us away from the enemy of the gods. Then they should worship the Sun with the mantra: "Beholding the light beyond the darkness, beholding the higher heaven, we have gone to Sūrya, the god among gods, the highest light.
If [the sun] has already set, they should worship the *āhavanīya* fire.

In that [fire], they should place fuel-sticks: the first with the formula, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper"; the second with, "Thou art a kindling-stick; may we prosper"; and the third with, "Whatever sin we have committed, or whatever we have caused another to commit, by this fuel-stick we weave it together and wipe it away. They should worship that very [fire] with the verse: "O waters, today we have come to you; we have united with the essence. Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; unite me with splendor. Until the Atirātra sacrifice on the day of the Udayanīya, in the case of Sattras, the day concludes with the Apsuṣoma cup.
14. Among those who eat curd-rice, including the *antama* and the *ahīna*, for as many days as they might consume the king, for that long they should not give the remains to a non-Brāhmaṇa. 15.
Or, having sprinkled them with water, they may give them. 16.
Regarding this, there is this verse: "O Brāhmaṇas, drink this Soma; eat whatever you may eat. Do not give the remnants to a Brāhmaṇa, lest one who does not drink Soma should drink the Soma.
(17) One should know this to be the circumambulation in all sacrifices. (18) This is the light. (19)
"All desires are indeed desires" (6.4.12).
Thus ends the fourth section of the sixth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
Thus ends the second book in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 2.

When about to chant the *ṣoḍaśin* with the *sāman*, the *udgātṛ* shall sit according to his seat, go to the *havirdhāna* shed, and gaze at the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the verse: "From whom [the other]... (RV 8.78.2). This same procedure applies to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), and likewise if they should draw [the cups] during the two subsequent pressings as well.
A black horse should stand at the door of the eastern *sadas*, facing westward, according to Śāṇḍilya;
facing eastward at the western door, according to Dhānañjayya.
In the absence of a black horse, a brownish-black one may be used.
In its absence, any horse or bull; in the absence of a horse,
whoever recites a limb of the Sāman should hold gold.
The Udgātṛ [should touch the water] when they are about to reach the Nidhana;
or all [the priests] may touch it together.
As he descends, he should sing the first round (paryāya) in a low voice.
When it has set, the second [laud] is performed with a medium [chant];
when it has fully set, the third is performed openly.
When they perform the *upākaraṇa*, they should chant on that very day: [the first laud] covered by night and the [last] open.
One should give a horse and gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *udgātṛ* priest in rites where there are such fees.

(16) In that very *sattra*, they should consume the draught of the cup dedicated to Indra with the mantra "saha. (17) Having set it aside, they should do so if they chant the hymn with the *harivat* verses in the *aharika* meters. (18)
With the *anuṣṭubh* metre for the cup (19), or with the preceding [formula] (20).

Acting thus: "Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first partook of this portion of yours; I partake of it as their after-consumption (*anubhakṣa*). May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma"—[this is] for the draught-cup (21).
"Indram id dharī" (RV 8.97.12), says Śāṇḍilya; this means "let the goddess Vāc drink of the Soma," with an additional [verse]. 22.
At the *asatra* sacrifice, he should consume from the cup with "aindraḥ saha" (RV 10.112.9).
23. Gautama says that one should consume it at the *vājapeya* chant with the *triṣṭubh* metre. 24.

Dhānañjayya and Śāṇḍilya say that [the *hiṃkāra*] is with the *anuṣṭubh* metre (25). [The *hiṃkāra*] is with the *anuṣṭubh* metre during the night (26). They should utter the *hiṃkāra* at the juncture after each separate triplet of verses (27).
"The consumption [of the soma] is for those who have sacrificed with the *yajus*," [says the rule].
Gautama says it is for those *stotras* that exceed the *gāyatrī* metre.
Dhānaṃjayya and Śāṇḍilya say there are separate consumptions according to the sequence of the metres.
Either with the *anuṣṭubh* metre (31), or without metre (32),
or with a junction [of metres] (33).
Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. 1.
One who has established the sacred fires but has not yet performed a Soma sacrifice should perform the *paribhakṣa* after having caused another to perform the Soma sacrifice for him.
2. According to Śāṇḍilya, even one who is already a Soma-sacrificer [should do so].

Having offered the morning oblation, one should place the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and remove it toward the north. Having placed the drops into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, one should set it down near the Dakṣiṇa fire,
along with the wooden sword (sphyá) and a handful of darbha grass.

Having gone to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire and sat down behind the *āhavanīya*, he should take clarified butter into the *sruk* with the *sruva* spoon. As much as can be held, he should offer it with the mantra: "O Agni, forgive this our transgression; this path which we have come from afar—be thou a kinsman, a father, and a protector for those worthy of Soma; thou art the earth that makes mortals seers. Svāhā! (7) Having taken [butter] in exactly the same way, he offers it with: "Thou art the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the most beloved body of Agni, the most beloved oblation of Indra. Svāhā! (8)
Having taken the previous libations of clarified butter, he takes the last one of curd with the formula, "To the Viśve Devas, svāhā!

(9). Having poured the remainder of the curd into the ladle, he turns toward the north and consumes it with the formula, "O Soma, in thy vow, may we, fulfilling our minds within our bodies, obtain offspring. (10)

Having washed the *sruva* ladle, having returned by the same way he came, having placed the sacred thread over his right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and having touched water, he should sweep the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of the southern fire, sprinkle it with water, scratch it once with the wooden sword (*sphya*), place a fire-brand (*ulmuka*) upon it, spread *darbha* grass over it, pour water down upon it, and then pour out some of these drops, saying: "To the ancestral fathers of the lowest [class], who share in the draught, *svadhā*!"—this is the first [offering]. 11.
"To the Aurvas, the Kāvyas"—in this very same manner, separately toward the south. 12.
Having said, "O ancestors, rejoice here; drink according to your respective shares," he turns to the north, sits down, and remains as long as he thinks fit.
While turning back around, he should mutter: "The ancestors have rejoiced; the ancestors have not omitted their respective shares from the drinking of Soma.
He should then cast those Darbha grass blades and the drops of water into the Dakṣiṇa fire.
Thus ends the second section in the seventh chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.

Having put on the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*) and touched water, he should recite the following while going toward his home: "With a peaceful mind, I come to my human home. O house, do not fear; do not tremble. Bearing strength for me, may you likewise bear strength for him. With a gracious mind and a clear intellect, I come to the home with a divine thought. Those whose presence one seeks when traveling abroad, and in whom there is much goodwill—we invoke those homes. May they recognize us, as they know us; may the cattle, being invoked, be here."
"The goats and sheep have been invited, as well as the essence of food; they have been invited into our homes.

Having sat down behind the fire in the hall, he should recite: "May cattle be born here, may horses be born here, may men be born here; may even the one who bestows a thousand-fold sacrificial fee sit down here.
Having swept away the grass from around the fire, he should speak to his dearest friend.

He should release the cows among the cattle with the mantra: "May this mixing be mixed into these cows; may the bull's seed and your own vigor, O Indra, be mixed therein. "O Indra, let no one steal our cows; let no one steal their owner; let no man seeking friendship be a thief; let no robber have power over them. Those who are about to undergo initiation for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) should address one another thus: "Our good deeds shall be common, but our evil deeds separate. Whatever we have done in this session, and whatever we have done before, and whatever we shall do—let all that be as it has come to us."
If anyone among us should practice non-vow-observance, he shall not officiate at the sacrifice for those of us who are consecrated.
Indeed, in former times, people used to undergo consecration only after having recognized one another’s anger, verbal abuse, and hidden character for a full year.
From the time of their consecration onwards, their eating and sleeping were to take place in the master’s hall.

From the Upavasatha day onwards, they should restrain their speech at the Āgnīdhrīya fire; or rather, they should restrain their speech during the two junctions of day and night; they should speak only such words as end with the word *vicakṣaṇa*.
They should not offer salutations to anyone;
they should not converse with a Śūdra; and they should not warm themselves at a fire that serves as a sacred seat.
They should not exit through the western door of the hall of the master;
they should discharge their bodily excretions facing east or north;
and they should not speak much.
They should not show their teeth; they should not eat loudly; they should not eat what has not been offered.
One should not see them devouring one another;
they should partake of all the sacrificial offerings;
they should avoid anger and falsehood.
These observances [are to be kept] during the consecrations (dīkṣā),
or during both the consecrations and the attendant days (upasad), or until the end of the sacrificial session (satra).
They should avoid [these acts] at sunrise and sunset, during the *abhyāśrāvaṇa* call, and outside the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) when it has been spread out (28).
Thus ends the third section of the seventh chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. 1.
If any misfortune should befall these three, they should seek the consent (*upahava*) from the householder (*gṛhapati*).
If [the defect occurs] with the Udgātṛ, [he should offer it], for it is said: "The Udgātṛ is indeed Prajāpati for the sacrificer.
Or rather, [it may be offered] by all [the priests] in the sequence of their consecration.
When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried away, they should go to sleep.

If any one among them should die, they should carry him out by a way other than the regular path and cremate him using the common fire (*āhārya*), provided he was not a maintainer of the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). The same applies to his wife.
