Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), they should carry him out by the *āpnāna* way and cremate a maintainer of the sacred fires using the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*).
For the middle turn of the night, there should be the *hotṛṣāman* of Daivodāsa, or the *aurdhvasadmana*.

The variations of the Jyotiṣāmayaṇa:
1. Therein, that which is at the beginning and at the end is above the equinox (viṣuvat). 2.
When, month by month, the Trikadruka days are placed in the position of the first Abhiplava, it is the Nakṣatra sacrifice deficient by thirty-six [days]. 3.

For there are twenty-seven months; in the place of the first *abhiplava* [of the four-month period], there is the *jyotis-gauḥ-jyotis* [arrangement], and in the rotation it is *jyotis* alone; that is the thirteenth month, deficient by nine, which is purely sidereal (*nākṣatra*). In the even-numbered months, in the place of the first *abhiplava*, there is that five-day period (*pañcāha*); that is the lunar (*cāndramasa*) month, deficient by six.

In the sixth [month] and so forth, one should place the *trikadruka* and the *abhiplava* [days]; that is the eighteen-fold [sacrifice], the full-moon [offering] as the impulsion, belonging to the sun in the southern course (*tairyagayanika*).

Restraining their speech and closing the door, they should remain seated until the stars have appeared.

(23) When the constellation has been announced, Dhānañjayya says that they should go out by the eastern door and release their speech with the *subrahmaṇyā* formulas and the syllable *oṃ*. (24) Śāṇḍilya says that they should do so as soon as they hear the call being made. (25)

In the *ahīna* sacrifices, the sacrificer alone should perform the choosing of the priests (*vara-varaṇa*) and the restraining of speech (*vāgyamana*). Having performed [these], the others [the officiating priests] should act as required; having performed [these], the others should act as required.
Thus ends the fourth section in the ninth chapter of the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
Regarding the Mahāvrata: once the Pṛṣṭha-stotra has been introduced, Bhāṇḍitāyana says that one should sing the Parimāda hymn after yoking the Stoma.
Gautama and Śāṇḍilya, as well as Dhānañjayya, say that one should do so after taking up the two blades of grass and unyoking [the Stoma].
Some say [this should be done] even before the commencement of the Stotra.
Having gone to the south of the Āgnīdhrīya fire and to the north of the [main] fire, they should worship with the *prāṇa* formulas and so forth; this is stated in the Brāhmaṇa.
The Udgātṛ should chant each verse once, and the other two should join in the *nidhana*.
Furthermore, one should chant the *stobha* for every foot in the middle and at the endings, where the beginning and end are obstructed;
having returned by that same way, [one chants] the tail.
On the two sides of the vow, they should worship the southern wing with the first [verse] and the northern armpit as well;
they should insert Vasiṣṭha’s invocation with the words "O All-Gods."
Having approached the *cātvāla* pit and gone north of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed, they stand behind it;
according to Dhānañjayya, they face west from that very spot.
They should perform the final *nidhana* chant of that [sāman] until the exhaustion of their breath.
To the east, they face westward in front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds; behind them, they do so with the other [shed].
Looking from that very spot toward the *mārjālīya*, they recite "In the vault, the eagle... as used for the *dvandva* rites.
As it is with the *havirdhāna* sheds, so it is with the *sadas*.
Dhānañjayya says that they should stand facing west within the altar toward the Gārhapatya fire;
Śāṇḍilya says they should remain standing by the very same path as that [fire]. They should perform the Nidhana visibly, beginning with the word "Indra."
Thus ends the first section in the tenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. Now, one should equip the King (Soma). He should have two chariots, worthy of a king, as his followers.
Others should prepare the sacrificial ground to the east; from there, they should go around by the south.
Having gone to the east of the wife’s hall, the Udgātṛ should spread eastward-pointed darbha grass at the southern edge of the altar and cause him to sit upon it facing east.

Then he should bring him a coat of mail, or if someone else brings it, he should consecrate it with the mantra: "Arise, O King! Thy armor is on; thy chariot is yoked with horses, stretched out by the gods, and its axle is unbroken. As a king, become a protector of the people and of the Brāhmaṇas.

Having said, "Go around by the west," and having returned by that same way, he should station him at the northern edge of the altar and say: "Bind on thy hand-guard, make thy bowstring thy weapon, prepare three arrows made of iron, and let there be yet another as a fourth."
"Set it up," he should say.

As he is setting it up, he should address him with the mantra: "Set up the peg for Vaiṇāvata; do not let it fall away, lest it fly off—to guard the Brahman, for support, and to hold it fast—having gathered it together, stand firm. He should say this.
To the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-shed, they should fasten two skins, one in front and one behind, leaving a path for the chariot to the south.

He should say to him: "Go around the sacrificial ground clockwise; pierce the first skin as you approach, and with each subsequent arrow, pierce them one after another without missing. Let the others go toward the second skin as they please. After piercing the third, proceed northward. Then, with the fourth arrow, shoot in whichever direction you think best, saying: 'Slay those who hate the Brahman! Having seen the cows, you should stop; there they will let you rest."
Having addressed the Brahmin in this manner, they should cause him to make the sound *hiṅ* at the proper time;
thus ends the second section in the tenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
One should go toward the earth-drum (*bhūmidundubhi*). 1.
To the west of the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar, half of the pit for the Śvabhra should be dug within the sacrificial ground (antarvedi) and half outside the sacrificial ground (bahirvedi).
It should be covered with the hide of a bull, with the hair facing upwards. "Thou art speech. 4.

"O Dundubhi, speak ill of those who have reviled us at the sacrificial session while we were exhausted and seated in consecration; speak success to them, but speak success to us! "Drive away the hater, drive away the terrible voice; O Dundubhi, speak to us a friendly voice, auspicious fame! "Drive away the speech of the hater, he who is evil-hearted and treacherous; then, O Dundubhi, speak to us of prosperity, success, and glory! With these mantras, having struck [the drum] separately with the tail-hair (*bāladhāna*), one should consecrate another person who is being beaten.

Having touched water and having returned to that same place, they should stand behind it and worship the fire with these [formulas], according to the respective parts: "Homage to your Gāyatra, that which is in front; homage to your head, that which is in the east; homage to your Rathantara, that which is on the south, that which is your right wing; homage to your Bṛhat, that which is on the north, that which is your left wing; homage to your Yajñāyajñīya, that which is behind, that which is your tail; homage to your Vāmadevya, that which is your self, that which is your middle. Thus, they worship the individual limbs according to their significance.

Then, having performed everything in its entirety, [he should pray]: "O auspicious one, may we be very auspicious for you! You are the Name; may I become the Name! You are manifest; make me manifest! O Savitṛ, impel us toward prosperity! May I prevail over those among whom you behold human beings; bestow glory upon me! (7) Having thus performed the worship, they should enter the Sadas hall.
By another door, they should carry out a stool made of Udumbara wood with a frame of Muñja grass;
in the absence of Udumbara, [the stool] should be made from a sacrificial tree,
and in the absence of Muñja, it should be made of Darbha grass.
Its feet are a span (prādeśa) long;
the other limbs are a cubit (aratni) long.
Having offered an oblation on the Audumbarī post with the right hand, they should place it to the north of that post.

The Udgātṛ, having gone to the north of her and sat down behind her, should touch her feet while they touch the ground, having placed *kūrca* grass-mats beneath them, with the following formulas, addressing each limb separately: "The *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* are your two fore-feet; the *Śyaita* and *Naudhasa* the two hind-feet; the *Vairūpa* and *Vairāja* the two longitudinal ones; the *Śākvara* and *Raivata* the two transverse ones. Having touched the couch, he should say: "The *Ṛcs* are the longitudinal supports; the *Yajus* formulas are the crosswise supports; the *Sāmans* are the coverlet; prosperity (*śrī*) is the pillow; the dialogues (*vākovākya*) are the over-layers; the *Vāravantīya* chants are the joints; the *Rājana* is the self; and the *Yajñāyajñīya* is the foundation."

Having touched it with his mouth, chest, and both arms, he should ascend [the throne], saying: "May the Vasus ascend you with the Gāyatrī metre; I ascend after them for the sake of sovereignty (*rājya*). May the Rudras ascend you with the Triṣṭubh metre; I ascend after them for the sake of over-sovereignty (*vairājya*). May the Ādityas ascend you with the Jagatī metre; I ascend after them for the sake of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). May the Viśve Devas ascend you with the Anuṣṭubh metre; I ascend after them for the sake of supreme sovereignty (*sāmrājya*). (9)

Then, with these very [verses], he should cause the deities to ascend him, removing the word "kingdom" [from them], saying: "With this metre I mount thee," using the Vairāja as the fifth, according to Gautama;
with four, according to Dhānaṃjayya;
with three, according to Śāṇḍilya.
Having ascended, he should recite: "Sit upon this; sit upon this giver of happiness. Homage be to you; do not harm me.

(13) As he ascends it, the *praṣṭhī*, the *brahmán*, and the *gṛhapati* should ascend the *kūrca* seats. (14) The material for the seat has been explained; the material for the *vāṇa* [has also been explained]. (15)
Thus ends the fourth section in the tenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
Thus the third book of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra is completed.
It should be covered with a red bull’s hide, with the hair on the upper side.
In its ten rear openings, ten strings each should be fastened—made of muñja grass or darbha grass.
Regarding this, Śāṇḍilya says there should be three: thirty-four in the middle one, and thirty-three on each side.
In front, having divided those [strings] into three groups of three each, he should pull them upward one by one with the formulas "bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," and "svaḥ" respectively.

He should touch it with the words: "Speak, speak! O speaker, wide speaker, broad, easy of access, easy of passage, acting, causing action, acting, desiring to act, overcomer of fear, and one who causes fear to be overcome; subduer of the adversary, and slayer of the adversary; victorious, more victorious, powerful, and overpowering; possessing lofty speech, possessing great speech, possessing equal speech, and possessing great speech—speak forth the divine voice, which is Aindri, vast, multiform, and long-lived, for a hundred years! (5)
"May he draw out the loose threads; by these threads of ours, O bowstring, speak here of a hundred successes! We have succeeded, we have all crossed over; living, may we attain the light!

(6) Having recited this—"Speech is everything, the mind is the light, the mind is auspicious"—he should play [the instrument] with a reed-stalk (*iṣīkā*) and a branch of the cane-plant (*vetasa*) together with its leaves. (7) That which is naturally curved at the base is "endowed with Indra" (*sendraṇatā*). (8)
With the words "For the out-breath (prāṇa) thee," he should scratch upwards; with "For the in-breath (apāna) thee," downwards.

With "For the diffused breath (vyāna) thee," having scratched three times, he should throw the arrow towards the north after addressing the Brāhmaṇa with the formula: "While scratching this, may you [the arrow] not bite. Thus ends the first section in the eleventh chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
"Let the beaten drums resound; let the lutes play!"—thus he should say.
(1) At the eastern door, outside the *sadas*, there are a gourd-lute (*alābu-vīṇā*) and two curved *kapiśīrṣī* lutes.

(2) He should consecrate these—the two curved *kapiśīrṣī* lutes, the *kapiśīrṣī* lutes, the drums, and whatever musical instrument there may be—with this mantra: "Whatever sound there is, great and most mighty, by that may you proclaim our success. (3)
Regarding the *mahāvīṇā* and *piśīlavīṇā*, Gautama and Śāṇḍilya say they should be inside [the hall], while Dhānañjayya says they should be outside.

4. One should consecrate the *alābuvīṇā* and the *piśīlavīṇā* with the mantra: "May the *alābuvīṇā* and the *piśīlavīṇā*, by that mantra which they mastered, sing this in accompaniment; they shall magnify this *sāman*. 5.
Behind the singers, each wife should play two *kāṇḍavīṇās* and two *picchorās* alternately. 6.

Near the mouth, by means of striking a pipe made of reeds, they call those [instruments] *apaghāṭilās*. He should consecrate them with the mantra: "May that *apaghāṭilā* which the wife shall play softly drive away the enemy and the hater, [making him] like a tree-stump."

Looking over everything, he should mutter: "The wailing cries, the ulūlayas, the shouts, and whatever it stirs—all that is the success of the sacrifice; thus is this sung. (10) He should indeed mutter: "I am Suparṇa, Garuḍa; I shall utter this speech which will bring much about, which will cause much to be done, which will lead me to heaven, which will lead these sacrificers to heaven. (11) Thus ends the second section in the eleventh chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 2.11.2.11.

A Brāhmaṇa who is an *abhigara* (one who sings praises) should sit facing west at the door of the eastern *sadas*; a *vṛṣala* who is an *apagara* (one who sings disparagement) should sit facing east at the western [door].
He (the *apagara*) should say, "These performers of the sacrificial session have not succeeded. The *abhigara* should say, "They have succeeded."
To the south of the *mārjālīya* fire, an Arya should stand within the sacrificial altar facing the south (4).
Outside the altar, a Śūdra should stand facing the north (5). In the absence of an Arya, any member of an Aryan caste may serve this purpose (6).

The two of them should stretch out a white, circular skin. The Śūdra stands to the east [of the fire]; the student (brahmacārī) stands to the east of the Āgnīdhrīya fire within the altar facing north; outside the altar, the unchaste woman (puṃścalī) stands facing south.
She should say: "O you of evil conduct! O you who have broken your vow! (duścaritin navakīrṇin).
"Fie on you, wretched woman, harlot, sweeper of the village, cleanser of the penis for every man!"—thus the student [should say].
(10) In this manner, he repeats it three times with alternating order.
(11) When all the ritual acts have been completed, he should recite that same *abhigara* three times. (12)
Having released [the staff], the Śūdra should run away;
he should cause him to fall down with that very same [staff].
A student may revile another as he pleases.

To the west, outside the altar and in an enclosed space near the Āgnīdhrīya fire, two couples of whatever castes they may be shall unite. The householders’ female slaves, or those who are beloved, having filled new water-carrying vessels, go around the Mārjālīya fire from left to right, saying, "Hem! Haimahā! This is honey, this is honey! There should be at least five, up to five hundred, or twenty-five.
They should play lutes for them as well;
they should fasten drums upon all the corners;
and they should cause voices to be raised one higher than the other, as many as they can reach.
The Ghoṣas,
as well as the Hiṃkāra, Anvabhighāra, and so forth, should be performed according to their purpose. All the Ghoṣas and the Kumbhinī vessels continue until the end of the Stotra.
Thus ends the third section of the eleventh chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
Regarding the twenty-fifth [sūkta], Gautama says that one should insert [the verses] during the final round (paryāya) of the twenty-fourth [sūkta] in the *paricara*.
Dhānaṃjayya says that the place for insertion is [at the end of] the entire [sūkta].
"At the place of insertion for the first [stotra]," says Śāṇḍilya;
"or, having praised with the Caturviṃśa-stoma, he should chant the middle verse of the triplet without the *ahiṃkāra*.
This is called the *āskanda*.

"One should not do that," says Śāṇḍilyāyana. (6) When the last *stotrīyā* verse has been introduced (*prastuta*), one should step down with the feet. (7) Together with the *nidhana*, one should place [the feet] upon the ground. (8)

When the sacrificial food (bhakṣa) is being brought forward, he should descend and mutter the verses in reverse order used for the ascent: "May Heaven and Earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they nourish us with their blessings. 6. Then, sitting down, they should chant the Stotra with the remaining portions. 10.
When the Udayanīya Atirātra has been completed, they should go down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 11.
They should rub themselves with their hands and join together;
whoever has a wife here should have her massage his back;
the Unnetṛ should bring them water.
Having risen, the householder should put on the Soma-vestment; the others should put on new, unwashed garments. They should complete the rite starting from the sprinkling with water.
They should go by one way and return by another, so that there may be no contact with evil.
(18) When the omentum of the Anubandhya cow has been offered, he should have his hair and beard shaved at the southern edge of the altar.
(19) When that rite is completed, having gone either eastward or northward, those who have established the sacred fires should perform the Udavasānīya offerings separately. (20)
Those who have not maintained their sacred fires (anāhitāgni) should attend upon the householder who is performing the sacrifice.
Dhānañjayya says that they should offer oblations of cooked rice (sthālīpāka) dedicated to the respective deities of those fires.
They should live together for one year.
"Twelve nights, or a day and night,
or as long as they may press [the Soma], or as long as they may press"—
thus ends the fourth section in the eleventh chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
In all cases, Brahmā should stand to the south,
facing north, except for the homa offerings;
those sacrifices performed with a single fire are called *pākayajñas*.

While they are about to offer [the oblation], he should sit down very silently; once it has been offered, he may act as he pleases. He should also follow the sacrificial portions being carried away for the Śūlagava.
Standing to the south while the gifts are being deposited, and having touched water once they have been deposited, he should return without looking back. 7.
At a *pākayajña*, he should accept the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) silently, or with the words "Om. 8.
For an animal sacrifice, the sacrificial fee is indeed an animal. 9.
There should be a full vessel of the cooked sacrificial rice (sthālīpāka),
or of both [the rice and the milk], according to one's means;
one should not place a canopy behind [the altar].
Whatever sacrificial element he may be joined with, that he should repeat. (13) In all rites beginning with the *karman*, the Adhvaryu should cause the *praisha* to come forth.
(14) And he should enter by the eastern door, unless another is specifically prescribed. (15)

At the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), having entered by the southern door while they are about to pour out the fourfold-measure offering (cātuṣprāśya), he should sit down silently. (16) Once it has been poured out, he may act as required. (17) When they are about to take that [portion] away, he should do exactly the same. (18)
If they should cause it to be eaten by non-priests, they should take the rice grains and cast them away, saying, "The Neṣṭṛ has acted wrongly. Then they should set aside other [grains].
When the two fire-drills intended for the one about to establish the sacred fires have been handed over, the procedure should proceed according to the purpose.

In the forenoon, having gone to the south of the fire-places, he should cast away a blade of grass to the south where they are about to churn the fire, saying, "Expelled is Parāvasu. He should sit down, saying, "I sit in the seat of Āvasu.
[He should say] "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; Bṛhaspati is my Brahman, I am human, Om. With this formula he should sit down wherever it may be prescribed that one sits with a *yajus*.
He should follow the fire as it is being carried away;
once it has been set down, he should sit down with the Yajus formula.
Regarding this, Śāṇḍilya says that he should do so first.
"Dvitīyam" (the second), says Dhānañjayya.
One should sing the Rāthantara when [the fire] has been produced; the Vāmadevya while it is being carried forward. 28–30.
When it is stated, "One should sing all [verses] with the mind in the *tūca*s" (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.21), what else could possibly be understood as being performed with speech? (3.1.33)
Moreover, it is the singing itself that is prescribed for the Adhvaryu, not [the recitation] mentally (34).

Or rather, he should sing the secret (rahasya) hymns mentally; for the singing of those [hymns] which are to be sung in the forest does not take place in the village (35). According to Lāmakāyana, the Vāravantīya and the Yajñāyajñīya should be placed in the position of the first and the last [stotras] (36).
"In a former age it was so," says Śāṇḍilya (37).
Thus ends the first section of the twelfth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra. 1.
When about to churn [the fire], having taken hold of the two churning sticks, he should sing the *araṇī* [verse]. 1.
When [the fire] is being churned, one of these two [verses], "The men churn Agni... or "His smoke has risen, brilliant...", [is recited].
When it has burst into flames, [he recites]: "It has been seen, O Gātuvit... 4.

When the [sacrificial fires] are being established, the observance regarding the cows is the [recitation of] "agnim īḷe" (RV 1.1.1). Some maintain that these [verses] constitute the duty of the Udgātṛ priest, because of the Vedic statement:
"The Udgātṛ [performs] by means of the Sāmaveda."
Just as the *vihavya*, *sajaniya*, and *kayashubhiya* [stotras] belong to the Hotṛ and the Prastotṛ;
the *vairāja* and *śakvarī* [verses] are the *prastāvas*;
and because there is no specific injunction, they are performed by those who act as the Brahman priest.

For it is said that "from the performance of the ritual by the Udgātṛ, the four great officiating priests (mahartvijas) consume [the food]"; thus there is the consumption of the *cātuṣprāśya* (fourfold portion).
However, [it belongs] to the Brahman priest because of his authority, and because it is not prescribed for the office of the Udgātṛ.
And it is observed that he [the *udgātṛ*] performs the Sāman-singing, as in the passage: "Brahmā sings while standing upon the chariot wheel" (14).

Thus, the designation "*udgātṛ*" is a conventional term based on the majority of usage (15). Furthermore, within the *hautra* (the duties of the *hotṛ*), there are injunctions for the *vihavya* and other such hymns (16).
They chant the *prastāva* with *stotras* upon the *virāj* verses; for there is frequent scriptural authority stating, "They chant with the *purīṣa*" (ŚB 8.6.2.17).
There is no injunction [for these], because the injunction is twofold (18).
The application of the ritual action extends only as far as the explicit statement [of the scripture] (19).
When the final oblation has been offered, he should act according to the circumstances (20).
If they should offer oblations with dice, he should go there and sit down silently (21). By means of those [dice], he should act according to the circumstances in the game (22).
In all sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, he should sit down to the east of the sacrificer, facing the *āhavanīya* fire,
either at the junction of two enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) or at the tips of the offering spoons (*sruk*). 23–25.
Either the rubbish-heap (utkara) or the space between that and the Āhavanīya fire is the path for the sacrificer, but not for others.

When the Adhvaryu says to him, "O Brahman, I shall do this," he should respond with the mantra: "Impelled by Savitṛ, do that; Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; I am the human [Brahman]; Om! and thus give his assent.
This is the consecration for all [the vessels].
(29) "I shall do this aloud," [he says].
(30) While the *praṇītā* waters are being poured out, he should restrain his speech until their release. (31)

While those very [cows] are being led forth, [the procedure continues] up to the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), the *stambayajus*, and the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for the departure-offering (*prasthānīyā*);
or rather, wherever the Adhvaryu and the Bahvṛca (Hotṛ) perform their ritual actions;
or wherever they do not perform them, he should remain mostly silent.

Thus ends the second section in the twelfth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. If an expiation (prāyaścitta) must be performed, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the formula "bhūḥ svāhā"; into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with "bhuvaḥ svāhā"; and if it is during the Soma-pressing (sutyā), into the Āgnīdhrīya fire with "svaḥ svāhā"; and into the Āhavanīya fire with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā.
Having offered there, one should say: "We have performed the desired expiation."
If one should speak at an improper time, or if something un-sacrificial should occur, he should contemplate these very *vyāhṛtis*. 3.
"This [is] Viṣṇu," is the *varcas* verse. 4.
On the new moon day, they should purify themselves with the *doḥanapavitra* using the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. 5.
In the absence of that, [the vessel] should be made of Darbha grass in all sacrifices, according to Śāṇḍilyāyana.
As the Prāśitra is being brought forward, he should address it with the mantra: "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra."
Having sipped water, he should receive [the food] with the formula, "Thee, belonging to the god...
(VS 1.5). Having spread out blades of grass in front, he should set down the staff with the formula, "I set thee down on the navel of the earth" (VS 1.9).
Taking [the food] with his thumb and ring finger, he should eat it with the formula, "I eat thee with the mouth of Agni" (VS 1.10).
He should swallow it without chewing.
12. Having sipped water, he should place his hand on his chest with the formula: "I set thee in the belly of Indra. 13. Having washed the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, he should place it there. 14.
Or he may cause it to be brought back as it was taken; 15.
He should place the portion for the Brahman priest, once brought, in front of him; 16. When the sacrifice has been completed, he should consume it. 17.
One should carry the *anvāhārya* rice between the *brahman* priest and the sacrificer.
(18) If the *brahman* priest himself were to be the sacrificer, one should carry it to his front.
(19) Having carried it, one should silently touch him as he sits within the altar (*antarvedi*). (20)

"Thou art the portion of Prajāpati," or [alternatively]: "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk; thou art imperishable; for the sake of preservation, I take thee for preservation. Guard my out-breath and in-breath; guard my common breath and diffused breath; guard my upward-breath and form. Thou art vigor; bestow vigor upon me. At that very moment, he should cause the sacrificer to recite:

"May I prosper through thee in the presence of Prajāpati. Having come together, I shall give the Anvāhārya rice. O Brahman, you are the Brahman; I give thee for the sake of the Brahman. Protected today, do not harm me; being offered, be auspicious unto me."

the fourth book (prapāṭhaka) is completed. Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices: when they are about to cast away the *stambayajus*, one should sit down with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). 1.

Looking toward that very [Gārhapatya fire], we invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa Soma and with the hymns of the ancestors. There are cakes for the Traiyambakas, prepared on a single potsherd. Śāṇḍilya says that one should stand.

While standing at the *huta* (the offering), they should recite: "O Mother, we have appeased Rudra; we have appeased the god Tryambaka, so that he may make us prosperous, so that he may make us wealthier, so that he may make us rich in cattle, and so that he may inspire us with resolve. You are a remedy—a remedy for the cow, for the horse, and for man; a remedy for the ram and the ewe. May there be a good remedy.
(13) Thus ends the second section of the thirteenth chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. 2.
The sacrificer’s attendants, each taking a cake (*apūpa*), should circumambulate the fire three times, keeping it to their right. 1.
In that regard, Dhānaṃjayya says that one should recite the *parīya* mantra;

Śāṇḍilya says one should do so while standing. [The mantra is: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality. He should point out the desired object, saying, "From such-and-such a house.

In the same manner, they should walk around it three times.

Wherever the Adhvaryu causes them to stop, there they should stand and offer worship, saying: "This, O Rudra, is thy portion; with this as thy provision, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains, clad in a skin, with the Pināka bow in hand, and with thy bowstring unstrung."
They should mutter [the mantra] eleven times;
having touched water with the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ," they should return without looking back.
The office of the Brahman priest at the *haviryajña*s has been explained by the rules for the *varuṇapraghāsa*s.
While they are about to offer the oblation for the sacrificial posts (yūpāhuti) of the animals, he should sit silently. (14) When it has been offered, he may act according to his purpose.

(15) After the omentum (vapā) has been offered, having performed the purification (mārjana) at the Cātvāla pit with the formula "O waters, this [is yours]," he may act according to his purpose regarding the animals. (16)
While they are about to proceed with the *puroḍāśa* offerings, he should sit silently.

In that [water], they should touch water [with the mantra]: "O King Varuṇa, from every station, release us from that [sin]. (23) Thus ends the third section in the thirteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. From this point onward, the ritual begins with the sprinkling. (1)
They should not perform the worship of the sun.
When the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) is being offered, they should remain seated; once it has been offered, they may go about as they please.
If they should offer oblations of parched barley flour (saktu), they must remain seated until those oblations have been completed.
One should sit in the *āvrāja* position during the liquor-preparation rites of the *Sautrāmaṇī*.
There, they bring forward two fires; one should sit to the south of them.

(7) He should consume the draught of the Aśvins with [the mantra]: "The Aśvins have pressed [this] for you from the Asura Namuci; Sarasvatī has pressed it with power. This bright, honeyed, sparkling Soma-king, I consume here.
(8) If they should sprinkle the sacrificer with the remainder, he should rise up, go between the two fires, and, being addressed by the Adhvaryu, chant the *saṃśānāni*. (6)
One should chant the *stobha* on every foot [of the verse]. (10) While approaching the *nidhanas*, they should touch the head of the sacrificer.

In place of *śravasā*, [one uses] *jityā* for a Kṣatriya and *puṣṭyā* for a Vaiśya; so say some. (13) There are two Sautrāmaṇī sacrifices: the Kaukilī and the Carakasautrāmaṇī. There are seven forms of the *haviryajña*: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the *sautrāmaṇī*. There are seven forms of the *soma* sacrifice: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*.
Thus ends the fourth section of the thirteenth chapter of the *Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra*.
At the Soma-pressing, the ritual action prior to the Subrahmaṇyā litany is common to both the Brahman and the Udgātṛ. [The duties are:
1) looking at and stepping upon the altar;
2) the movement around, the worship of the fire-hearths (dhiṣṇya), the acceptance of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), and the consumption of the portions.
After the *stomavimocana*, the rest is the same.
However, at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering],
once it has been completed, the sacrificer must remain seated until the conclusion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*).

When the Adhvaryu restrains his speech, he should then remain silent until the purpose [of the rite] is accomplished. When they are about to collect the Mahāvīra vessels, he should sit silently; once they have been collected, he may act according to the requirements of the ritual.
While the *prāyaṇīyā* offering has not yet been completed, he should stand to the east of the wife’s hall until the oblation for the footprint of the cow that purchases the King (Soma) is offered.

Once the oblation has been offered, he should go to the north of the Soma-cart; or, if he has gone south before the oblation for the footprint, he should go to where they intend to purchase the King and sit down silently. When the King has been purchased, he should step forward to the east. Having caused the King to be placed [on the cart] by way of the west, he should follow it as it is being carried after it has been set down, provided he had previously gone by the south.

If it should turn back toward the west after being purchased in the north, they should carry it eastward and place it upon the King; having placed it, he should follow it as it is carried around by the west. 13. He should turn back along that very same path. 14.
For that [path] becomes his southern course while he is proceeding toward the east. 15.

When the *vimukta* has been released, he should step out to the south between the *somavahana* cart and the *patnīśālā* and stand there, provided he is initiated, until the carrying away of the King Soma. (16) He should enter following the King Soma as he is being brought in, not passing between the fires.
(17) If there should be a crowding, he may enter even by the southern door. (18)
If the consecrated person (dīkṣita) is present, he should pass between the Āhavanīya fire to the north and the sacrificial altar (vedi) to the west.
Thus ends the first section of the fourteenth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. 1.
They perform the guest-offering (ātithyā-iṣṭi). 1.

When it has been completed, they should murmur while touching the *tānūnaptra* clarified butter: "Thou art the oblation, belonging to Vaiśvānara, unassailed, unassailable, the vigor of the gods, beyond reproach, a protector against reproach; O thou who art beyond reproach, may we straightway attain truth and place ourselves in prosperity. Having touched water and being addressed by the Adhvaryu, he should release the King [Soma].

Placing that gold beneath [the Soma], they should touch it with the mantra: "O divine Soma, may you swell; may you swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize. (5) They should conceal themselves on a prastara made of *kāśa* grass, having placed their right hands upward and their left hands downward, with the formula: "Desired are riches, desired are boons; I send [this] to Bhaga. To those who speak the truth, homage! Homage to Heaven! Homage to Earth! (6)
When the Subrahmaṇyā calls are being uttered, if the sacrificer is initiated, he should step out toward the south and stand there;

The left-hand ones [the ladles] should be turned face upwards in the afternoon, while the right-hand ones should be turned face downwards. When the *upasat* oblation has been offered with the *sruva*-ladle, one should know that the rite is concluded.

Thus ends the second section in the fourteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
Regarding those about to kindle the fire: having gone to the Gārhapatya, he should sit down with a Yajus formula to its south;
if [the fire-altar] is outside, he should sit to the north of the Dakṣiṇāgni.

After the oblation has been offered, he should cause the sacrificer to recite: "May the Aśvins drink the Gharma; may Heaven and Earth approve it. May the gifts remain right here. 6. When they are about to establish the Āhavanīya fire, one should sit down with the Yajus formula.

furthermore, some say it may be in seven forms because of the scriptural statement.

The *hiṃkāra* precedes the *prastāva*; the *udgītha* begins with the syllable *oṃ*. There are four types of *sāmans* characterized by uneven divisions (*viṣamabhakti*), distinguished by their words, *sastobhas*, and *stobhas*: namely, the *Pravad-bhārgava*, the *Mahā-vaiśvāmitra*, and the *Saumitra*.
The *avasāna* (caesura), characterized by the end of a *prastāva*, belongs to those [verses] that are indivisible;
it occurs at the end of two [padas], or before the *vāravantīya*,
or according to the former [rule].
The four-syllable [mantra] for those who have won through Kārṇaśravas, the bearer of strength; also for Surūpa;
and the word for Vājiga and others.
In the *eḍa* [sāman], there is a half-verse in the *sākamaśva* (15) and in the *śaukta* (16);
in the *ābhīśava* [sāmans], it occurs at the end of the *stobha* (17).
The practiced higher [mantra] is 18; ending with *hāu* for the purpose of causing to fall is 16;
in the mouth of Vāk it is 20.
The sixteen-syllable [mantra] of Nānada (21), as well as those of Gośṛṅga and Sañjaya (22),
and that of Daivodāsa at night (23).
The *ṛṣabha* of Raivata consists of thirty-six syllables (24).
For all [these chants], the commencement of the *udgītha* is with the syllable *oṃ* (25).
However, Dhānañjayya [prescribes] the omission of the first syllable, while Śāṇḍilya [prescribes] its non-omission (26).
Thus, in the second section of the eighteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra:
"The Sāman that has been introduced indeed sinks; the Udgātṛ supports it with the syllable Oṃ," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
One should either transform that very vowel among the vowels into the syllable Oṃ, or one should employ an adventitious Oṃ among the consonants.
Regarding those with reversed accents (pratyavetasvara):

one should apply whichever [accent] would harmonize with the direct (pratyakṣa), indirect (parokṣa), protracted (pracira), placed (nyasta), raised (ūḍha), acute (udātta), drawn out (kṛṣṭa), or not drawn out (akṛṣṭa).
However, everything should be done with the lighter [vowel], by means of the elision of a mora (mātrā).
The beginning of a word is the location for the *pratihāra* everywhere (6); and when there is no specific indication of a word, it is at the final word (7);
and in the case of numerical matters, the authority rests with the number of syllables (8).
Within the *pratihāra*, the *pratihartṛ* should utter the *stobhas*;

and those [stobhas] that follow after the *ṛc* verses, except for those separated from the *ṛc*. For those [verses] whose final *pāda* consists of eight syllables—except for the *paṅkti* meters—there are four [stobhas].

In that case, the designation "proper" (nyāyya) applies; 12. And [the term] "end of a word" (padānta), when used without qualification, should be understood as referring to the penultimate syllable of a word; 13.
This rule applies in the absence of a specific substitute (anādeśe). 14.
The Udgātṛ takes his portion for the *stobha* after the *pratihāra* of these: the *saumedhasya*, the *aurṇāyava*, the *ṛṣabha*, the *pāvamāna*, the *nidhana*, and the *mārgīyava*. 15.

For the *nyāyyapratihāra* *iḍās*, the *saṃkṣāra*, the *aśvasūkta*, the *iḍasvara*, the *vārṣāhara*, the *svāra*, the *kautsa*, the *gorāṅgirasa sāman*, and the *abhyāsavat krauñca*—for these, including the *agnimīya* [sāmans], the Pratihartṛ takes his portion before the *pratihāra*. 16–17. [These include] the *saṃhita*, the *ārṣabha*, the *śākala*, the *vājadāvarya*, the *svāra*, the *saumitra*, the *padanidhana*, and the *kāṇvarohitakūlīya*.

Thus ends the third section in the eighteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. In the *yauktāśva* [sāman], following the *sauparṇa* [sāmans], there are: the *yaudhājaya*, the *naudhasa* with the *āṣkāra* finale, the *kāṇva*, the *yauktasruc*, the *vāmra* with the *tīraścī* finale, the *āyāsya*, the *indrasya yaśas*, the *vaiṣṇava* with the *uttara* [finale], the *sapha*, the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*, the long *pauṣkala*, the *āndhīgava*, the *bṛhat* belonging to Agni, and the *śyāvāśva* and *traisoka*. Of these, two [are used]. (1) There is a preceding *stobha* for the first of the two *yauktāśva* [sāmans]. (2)
In the case of Śyāvāśva and Traiśoka, [the *udātta* accent] occurs at the end of the word (3).
However, for Śyāvāśva, it is not an *stobha* (4).
At the end of the word, it is appropriate [to apply it] in the Vāma [recension] (5).
The *viśoviśīya* [sāman] begins with the syllable *oṃ* by means of the third and fourth [verses], for it is indeed so;
or else it begins with *hiṃ* by means of the fifth and sixth [verses]. The *śaukta* and *nārmedha* [sāmans] have two *pratihāra*s.
The first and ninth [verses] belong to Śaukta;
the final [verse] belongs to Nārmedha with four [syllables], and the subsequent one with the same four middle [syllables].
Or, there is a single *pratihāra* with the latter [verse].
The end of the pādas of the Gāyatra-sāmans Bhāsa and Vairūpa [is marked] by two [syllables] for Bhāsa,
and by four for the latter.
With the third *pada*, there are ten [syllables] in the *sauhaviṣa* finale of the *yajñāyajñīya* (15),
and in the *śrāyantīya* and *vāruṇasāman* of the *dvaigata* (16).
Of these, for the first two, the entire *pada* and two [syllables] of the repeated portion [are to be omitted] (17).
In the case of *dvaigarta*, however, [the first syllable] is doubled at the end of a word (18). In the case of *rañjas*, the beginning of the penultimate word is doubled (19).
For the nine words beginning with *viśoviśīya*, the first syllable of the final word is optionally doubled (20).

The final syllable ending in *hāi* belongs to the *viśoviśīya*; 21. The beginning of the repetition belongs to the *śrāyantīya* and the *varuṇasāman*; 22. Or there are four [syllables] before the *hiṃkāra*, [repeated] before each *hiṃkāra*. 23.
Thus ends the fourth section (khaṇḍa) in the eighteenth chapter (paṭala) of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.

Thus ends the sixth book (prapāṭhaka) of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. The Vāmadevya, the Svāra, the Sākamaśva, the Pāṣṭhauha, the Nidhanakāma, the Satrāsāhīya, the Kākṣīvata, the Cyāvana, the two Gāyatrīsāmans, the Auśana, the Nidhanavat, and the Aidhmavāha—among these, the fifth and the sixth are optionally substituted according to what is appropriate.

The *gūrda* [is] the *saumedha*, the *mādhucchandasa*, the *audala*, the *sauśravasa*, the *uttara*, the *vārtratura*, the *ṛṣabha*, the *raivata*, the *kautsa*, the *auṣṇiha*, the *ātīṣādīya*, the *krośa*, the *ekonidhana*, the *svāra*, the *sāmarāja*, the *māruta*, the *auṣṇiha*, the *ākṣāra*, the *sujñāna*, the *hārivarṇa*, the *sāṃvarta*, the *jāgata*, the *varuṇasāma*, the *marutāṃdhenu*, and the *sraugmata*. Of these, there are four repetitions of the *gūrda*; three repetitions, beginning with the first, for the remaining three.
The *uttamāni* [verses] are for the sake of renown (5);
or eight [are recited] for the slayer of Vṛtra (6); and the two preceding ones are to be applied according to the rule (7).
The middle [pitch] is for Ṛṣabha (8);
the middle [pitches] are for the five following [notes] (9);
or, according to Kautsa, the highest [pitches] are used before repetition (10).
Or there is a *stobha* before the first [verses] of the *Sāmarāja*;
or six [verses], beginning with the fifth, in the *Māruta*;
five [verses] in the *Aśva* and *Rathantara*.
In the Vaidanvata and in the Abhyāsavat [stomas],
[the *praṇava* is placed] at the end of the final word; but in the Uttama [stoma], it is at the beginning, or else two [are placed] on both sides in the Ubhayataḥstoma.
"Or the third [verse]," "both," or "one"— thus ends the first section in the nineteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 1.17–18.1.

The Ākūpāra and Krauñca are *gāyatrī* *sāmans*; the Daivātitha, Gauṣūkta, Raurava with two *hiṃkāras*, Vāmadevya with the *prastāva* ending in the syllable *ekāra*, Vaiyaśva to be sung in the forest (*araṇyegeya*), Śākvaravarṇa, Saubhara, Bārhadgira, Āyovājīya, Svāra, Aidhmavāha, Gauśṛṅga, Hārāyaṇa, Kaulmalabarhiṣa, Janitra, the latter Vaitahavya, the *Vāmadevya* containing the word "here" (*ihavat*) with the *iḍā* formula facing westward, Kāśīta, Vaiṣṇava, and the former Śyaita and Saṃjaya. Of these, six [have no *stobhas*] at the end; two have no *stobhas* at the beginning and end; and two have *stobhas* on both sides at the first and third [verses].
Before the *aukāra* in the first [verse], before the *hiṃkāra* in the third,
and before the *apratihāra* in the preceding *stotrīya*, [one should recite] the syllable of the *śākvara*.
In this [section], there is a *stobha* after a word ending in *-i* in the case of *aidhmavāhaḥ* (7),
or it may apply to all [such words] (8).
In the three subsequent [sections], it applies to words ending in *-ā* (6).
And in the *paurumadga* [hymn],
from the syllable "o" in the *janitṛ* [verse],
together with the *vauṣaṭ* call, there is the *paurumadga*.
The final word of the *gauśṛṅga*, *hārāyaṇa*, *kaulmalabarhiṣa*, and *vaitahavya* [sections] may optionally [be joined with the following].

(13) [The *nidhana*] consists of two [syllables] for the two preceding [sections], and four syllables more for the two succeeding ones. (14) For the *kaulmalabarhiṣa* [section], there is a *stobha* before [the *nidhana*]. (15)
Thus, in the nineteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra, the second section:
there are seven [stotras] at the Vāravantīya; in the former [set], three are at the end of the *padas*:
the Kārṣaśravasa, the Traita, and the Pajra; the Tauraśravasa is the next; the Śrudhya is the son of Udvaṃśa; and the Śākvara [is the last]. Of these, there are eight.
Half-verses of the *pajra*, *tura*, and *aśrava* [verses] at the end of a foot;
3. and of the *śrudhīya* [verse] in *kakubh* meters; 4. four [half-verses] of that [same *śrudhīya*] in *gāyatrī* meters; 5.
There are sixteen [verses] in the *bṛhatī* meters;
"nadaṃ va odatīnām" consists of ten [verses]; there is a repetition of the middle *pada* in the *śākvara* [meter].

Or rather, the *abhikranda* of Vāyu is appropriate: the *svāra* [Sāman] for Kava, the *aurukṣaya* for Auśana, the *traiṣṭubha* for Yavāśva, the *śnauṣṭa* for Jāgata, the *somasāman* for Kārtayaśa, the *svāra* with the *payonidhana* for Ṛṣabha, and the *śākvara* for Yaṇvāpatya. Of these, the final foot of the last three has a *purastātstobha*.
The first *stotrīyā* verse of the two sons of Yaṇva is without a *pratihāra*. 12.
Of the five [verses], there are four syllables at the beginning of the last *pāda*. 13.
The *Vaikhānasa*, the *Pauruhanmana*, the *Udvaṃśīya*, and the *Āṣkāraṇidhana*—these are the *Tvaṣṭrīsāmans*. Of these, the last *pāda* precedes the repetition (*abhyāsa*). 14.
Or, in the case of repetition, there are four [stotras] for the two subsequent ones (15).
Thus ends the third section of the nineteenth chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*.

The *Śāktyasāman*, the *Maidhātitha*, the *Vāravantīya* as the second [stotra] for the *Ābhīśava*; the *Niṣedha* of the *Simās*, the *Tāṣṭrīsāman* with three *nidhanas* for the *Āyāsya*; the *Dārḍhacyuta* and the *Ātharvaṇa* for the *Revatīs*; the *Agni-trinidhana*, the *Utsedha-niṣedha*, the *Vaiḍa*, the *Sākamaśva*, the *Dairghaśravasa*, the *Dāśaspatya*, and the *Grāmegeya-Śyena*—these have two *pratihāras* each. 1.
In the case of the two middle *padas* of the *śāktya*, *sāman*, and *maidhātithi* [stotras],
the end of the *pada* is joined with either two or four [syllables] of the *ihāhe* and *vāravantīya* [stotras].
The *ekaprati-hāra* occurs with seven [notes] before the *āhāva*;
[the syllable] beginning with *u* is the end of a word with one [note];
or it is according to what is logical.
And for the two preceding [sāmans], there are four [verses] in place of seven of the *vāravantīya* in the *dvipadā* meters,
and two [verses] in place of four.
"Two [syllables] as one" refers to the single-footed [verse] (ekapadā); 11. "Of the two subsequent feet, [the syllables of] the subsequent [feet]" [are combined]; 12.
"But two by two" refers to the six beginning with the *ābhīśava*. 13.
There are four [verses] for the prohibition of the boundaries and for the Tvaṣṭṛ-sāman; or there are four preceding stobhas of the Atharvaṇa-sāman;
and there are four [verses] beginning with that.
Or there are eight [stobhas] in the Dāśaspatya;
or [there are eight] with a single *pratihāra* on the preceding [verse];
[there are eight] with the third and fifth *padas* in the Śyena.
In the fourth and sixth [verses], there are two [repetitions] of each pada;
thus says the fourth section of the nineteenth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
Regarding the separate stotriyas, the *pratihāras* are continuous (*saṃtaninaḥ*). 1.
Three each are on the udders of the Mahānāmnīs;
these they call the *pratitodas*.
Likewise, there are the *svaras* in the case of the *nityavatsā* and the *atisaṅgī*.
But for all [of these], there are two each;
or six, excluding the *saṃtani*;
[this applies] to the *mahānāmnī*s among the *śākvara* and *uttama* [stotras].

In the sixth [section], there are eight *āndhāsvara* middle verses; the *stotriya* verses are in the *purīṣa* sections; there are six [verses] without *pratihāra*; and the teachers say that the *adhyāsa-parīṣa* sections consist of ten words.
Of these, the first and second verses are *dvipadā*s (11);
there are three *śākvara* verses (12);
[the words] "dhātu," "vatsa," and "ūdhas" (13).
"that Śākvara," "14," "man," "three," "Śākvaras," "having sat upon," "15"—
these are the words. 16.
The *uttamā* [verse], however, is a double superimposition (17).

Regarding the *dvipadā* verses, the *prastāva* is stated by Bhāsa to be at the end of the words in the *śākvara-prathama* verses and in the *purīṣa* words (18). In the *yajñāyajñīya*, it is at the end of the word in the *devasthāna* section, according to the *vairūpa* [sāman] (19).
The *araṇyegeya* hymns are the *Śyena*, the *Pārthuraśma*, and the *Acchidra-ṛṣiṣṭha*. Of these, in the latter [hymns],
there are two [verses] each in the first two [sections],
and four each in the latter two.
The *stobhas* of the *Pārthuraśma* [Sāman] are on both sides; 23.
for the *Vairūpa*, the *nidhanas* are "devatāpadam, devatāpadam"; 24. the *pratihāra* consists of *stobhas* prior to the *Śiśumatī*. 25.
The eleventh [verse] belongs to Aiḍa Daivodāsa (26);
the seventh and eighth belong to Traikakuba (27);
the ninth and tenth belong to Vaiśvamanasa (28).

Likewise, in the case of the *vṛṣṇa* [stotras], one should divide the words individually in all chants that have similar melodies (*sadṛśagīti*), based on the repetitions of those [words] uttered three times. In the absence of a specific instruction regarding the end, the *udgātṛ* should perform the remaining divisions; these are the parts to be divided.
Those [sāmans] not specifically designated are based on the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters (32).
And those with many syllables, stobhas, and so forth are found in the secret texts (*rahasya*) (33).

For example: Vasiṣṭha’s *vairāja* with the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its *nidhana*; the *mahāvaiśvamitra* for Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra; the *saumitra* with the *svar* as its *nidhana*; the *daivodāsa*, the *aiḍa*, the *vaidanvata*, and the *plava*; the *parītoyonīni*; the *krauñca*; the *tvāṣṭrīsāman*s; the *svāra* with the *vāc* as its *nidhana*; and the *ākūpāra* with repetition (34).
In the *stobhas* at the beginning and end, one should chant *stobha* for every word (*pada*). Whichever word one may utter, so it should be chanted in the *anupada-stobhas*.
Thus ends the first section in the twentieth chapter of the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*.
The *pratihāra* [section] consists of *stobhas* occurring before the fourth *pada*.

Those [verses] whose *nidhanas* are *padas* similar to the *upāya* and which end with *stobhas* are called *stobhavibhājyas*. In that case, the *pratihartṛ* should perform the *stobha* specifically for the third *pada*.
The *stobha*s of the single bull possess skillful means;
they belong to the bull among the gods, the possessor of power (*śākvara*).
They should perform these with various *stobha*s.
If the *prastāva* and *pratihāra* are to be divided within a word that includes the syllable "deva," then,
according to Dhānañjayya, one should perform the *pratihāra* after leaving the last divisional section (*vyāvarga*) remaining in the *gāyatrī* *sāmans* when they are to be divided.
According to Śāṇḍilyāyana, however, one should do so with the entire word.
In the *śukriya* chants, they should recite the *stobhas* three times, except for the *nidhanas*.
(11) In the introductory section of the *mahādivākīrtya*, one should transpose the two deities.
(12) Thus, it will become a journey characterized by light and a departure characterized by light. (13)

In that case, the self is the one who shares in the *stobha* (14). The *prastotṛ* should chant the first *anugāna* for himself as well (15). All other *anugānas*, however, the *udgātṛ* alone should recite (16).
They should follow him at their respective terminations (nidhanas).
Or, having brought back the last three *anugānas*, they should join them with the others from their own positions according to the rule of *stobha*.

Another view is that those [verses] which were before the *ātman* at the beginning should be performed once, and those which are after it at the end should be performed once; thus one should complete the *stoma* by means of the *ātman* itself.
At the beginning and end of the *paryāyas*,
or at the *viṣṭāvas*,
the Udgātṛ alone should state the means for the tenth foot at the conclusion of the *bhāsas*.
All [verses] recited three times by the *rājana* singer, they should recite five times; 23. after each of those, there are *stobha* interjections; 24. the *prastāva* is performed on each *pada*. 25.
The *pratihāra* is performed with the third *pada* together with the preceding *stobha* (26),
or it may be divided (*vibhājyam*) (27).
In that case, if there is a *pada* immediately preceding [the third], they should recite these [syllables] together with it (28).
Some say that one should cause the deity of the word to tremble (vyavastobhet). 26.
In the *padastobhas*, the *nidhanas* are the words; likewise, the *iḍās*. 30.
From these, they should chant various *stobhas*. 31.
The Prastotṛ [sings] for the first three [verses]; the Pratihartṛ [sings] for the seventh and the following three [verses].
(32) In the case of those [verses] separated by the *iḍā*, half a foot is the *nidhana*. (33) In the case of those not separated, the whole [verse] is [the *nidhana*]. (34)
The first quarter-verse of the fourth [prapāṭhaka] consists of four three-syllable units as its *nidhana*s;
the third is likewise;
or else the second and last [quarters] are divided in two, each consisting of four syllables.
If they are indivisible, [the first] is [completed] by the eighth *stobha*, the others by the ninth, and the last by the tenth. 38, 36, 40.
The introduction for all [the verses] is by the first [verse], 41. Thus ends the second section (khaṇḍa) in the twentieth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
There are six [verses] in the final *anugāna* of the *ilānda*, 1.
The others are to be divided;
or rather, the first is to be divided;
there, by means of a middle utterance for the highest *stobha*.
There are eleven [verses] for Dīrghatamas;
with the eighth *stobhas* recited three times, there is [attainment of] fortune and excellence;
and if there are two *pratihāras*, it is by means of the fifth [syllables].
In the division of the *stobha*s according to the five syllables, there are the *dharma* and *vidharma* [sections] (8);
or it may take the form of two feet (6).
The *pratihāra* for these two is performed with the tenth *stobha*s (10).
And if there are two *pratihāras*, [the *nidhana*] is with the sixth [note]; if at the end of a word, it consists of three [syllables], as in the *sauhaviṣa* [chant], or at the beginning of a word.
The middle verse is [used] for the Svarṇidhana and the Sauhavisa;
or it may be divided.
The middle verse alone is the stobha preceding the Vairāja.
They should repeat its final words four times; likewise for the Vātsapra of the fourth day, but [only] the *samādhi*. 17–20. 30.
Lāmakāyana [places] the *ṛc* and so forth at the end;
Śāṇḍilya [places] the *stobha*; and [the view beginning with] Padādi applies to the *traikakubha*.

In the case of those [stotras] that are indivisible, before the means [of the Prastāva], one should respond with the *vyāvarga* (division) in six or eight [syllables], or as in the *vāmadevya* and *krośa* [sāmans]. Regarding this, Śāṇḍilya says it should be with the former division, while Dhānañjayya says it should be with the latter. The *pratihāra* in the *vaicchandasa* [sāmans] is indeed the song itself as the response.
This applies even at the beginning of a word.

Gautama says that one should take up [the *pratihāra*] from the beginning of the *pratihāra* with the syllable *oṃ*. (26) However, for those [sāmans] that have returned [to the *nidhana*], one should respond with the *svaras*; as in the case of the Kāleya, Vātsagurda, and others.
(27) Or [it may be] for those that do not perform the *nakāra*, or for the *maya*, or for the *vara*. (28)
Dhānañjayya says that one should take up the syllables whose vowels have been reversed by means of the syllable *oṃ*.
Śāṇḍilya says according to the traditional recitation (*yathāmnāyam*).
