for it says of the Ādityas, 'one should buy it immediately,' but not of the others."
On the following day, there is the rite called the *anukraya* (subsequent purchase).
Dhānañjayya maintains that the preceding day should end with the *upavasatha*.
For he says, "Tomorrow is the *sutyā*"; had it been otherwise, he would have said, "They announced the purchase for tomorrow."

By the phrase "he purchased it immediately," [the text] shows the immediate nature of the first [purchase]. However, because it was two days later, the Aṅgirasas purchased it at a later time; therefore, it is called "anukrī" (purchased subsequently).
Of that [purchase], a horse is the one-hundred-and-first among the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); for the horse is indeed speech.
By this, the Viśvajit, the Śilpa, and the Dvirātra have been described;

Dhānañjayya says it is a Tryaha-ahīna sacrifice. The first day is the consecration (daikṣa), the second extends from the purchase [of the Soma] until the Upavasatha, and the last is the pressing day (sautya).
He should give him as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) riches according to his enthusiasm, whatever may be most highly desired in that region. 17.
Dhānañjayya says that he should give everything he possesses. 18. [The gifts are:
a measured bed, a ladder, a pair of slaves in the kitchen, a measure of grain, a plough, and a cow. 19.
Thus ends the fourth section in the twenty-second chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
For the Śyena sacrifice, one should choose as officiating priests (ṛtvij) the sons of those who observe vows and those who are warriors, provided they are learned in the Vedas;
Dhānañjayya, however, maintains that only those who are truly worthy should be chosen.
One should churn clarified butter from those plants that are not blown upon by the wind while others around them are being blown upon.
Or, they should make the sacrificial ground where thickets or trees have grown densely and cut them down. Or, it may be a naturally hollowed-out depression.
"On the two naves of the pressing-boards" (6).
On the two pressing-boards of whatever vehicle they might carry out the deceased, they should fashion [the marks] on its two naves.
"The top of the wooden sword shall be the part for the *caṣāla*" (8). And thus, the portion for the *caṣāla* should be at the tip of the wooden sword.
The officiating priests (ṛtvij) proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with their sacred threads suspended over the right shoulder; they are accompanied by men bearing uplifted bows. 9.

One should perform the Rathantara chant during the Pavamāna laud; it should be placed in the position of a single verse within the Bṛhatī meter, for that is the position belonging to verses in the Bṛhatī meter.
10. And in this way, it occurs in a triplet (tṛca). 11.

One should arrange the others without contradiction; thus there is yet another minor modification. (12) Therein, one should employ the fifth [verse] as belonging to the Bṛhatī meter according to the requirement of the *stoma*.
(13) That should be the *paurumadga* [sāman], for it shows the slaying of the enemy therein. (14)
"The teachers say that there should be two *dvipadā* verses of the *rathantara* on the [first] two *pṛṣṭha* days, for the scripture says, 'in the forward direction' (*parācīṣu*).
Gautama, however, says they should be two *kakubh* verses,
because this shows the non-return of the *stoma*."
While performing the *plava* as the *brahmasāman*, one should perform it upon these *ṛc*s.
For in this place, no subsistence (*vṛtti*) for the *pāvamānī* verses is found.
One should give nine groups of nine sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability. [This applies] to those who are one-eyed, lame, humpbacked, or maimed.

They should cause blood to flow for them toward the southern boundary. (21) In the case of the Ekatrika sacrifice, they should perform everything on the same day. (22) Gautama says that there should be one initiation and three Upasad days. (23)
Its Gāyatra-side [stotra] is the Ārbhava-praüga with the verses beginning "ayā rucā.
Śāṇḍilya says it belongs to the Purojiti [sāman].
One should place the verse "sasunve yo vasūnām" in the middle of that [Purojiti].

Regarding the verse, "He goes toward the eastern quarter, being observant," one should perform the *udvaṃśīya* chant upon this [verse], having lifted up the side of the *gāyatra*, according to Lāmakāyana (27).
Śāṇḍilya says that the *bahiṣpavamāna* should consist of three verses (28).
The midday [stotra] should have five verses, the *ārbhava* seven, and the others should have one less (29).
Some [chapters] consist of three triplets, such as the *hotṛṣāman* and the *pavamāna* hymns; or they are completed by adding four verses at a time.
Two by two, in groups of three and five,
through his descent, that constitutes his sixtieth [offering]; these are the sacrificial gifts, the sacrificial gifts.
Thus ends the fifth section in the twenty-second chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.

Those intending to sacrifice with the Vrātyastoma rites, having separately established their sacred fires and prepared the sacrificial implements, shall undergo initiation at the *gārhapatya* fire of that one among them who is most distinguished in Vedic study, or by lineage, or—in its absence—by the acquisition of wealth;
and they shall consume their portions of the sacrificial food together.
Because the strength of the performance preceded by the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is superior after one has sacrificed with the *jyotiṣṭoma*, as it is said:
"That sacrificial rite is the Dakṣiṇā; there are five Dakṣiṇās.
However, since these [sacrifices] are not completed from Indra, therefore they are not authoritative.
Because of the statement of a fault regarding [the sacrifice] even after it has been performed without having been commenced; because of the injunction for the *vrāta* and the *pratipad*;
and just as the *agnyādheya* [is prescribed] for those who are impure.
The *upahavya*, the *agniṣṭut*, and the *mīmāṃsita-sattra* should be performed again; furthermore, there should be *stomas* that have not yet been sacrificed with.
Whatever *vrātyas* may assemble together, they should sacrifice with the first [of these].
The others have been described by the Brāhmaṇa.

Those who have lost their virility and ceased procreating, whose testicles have shriveled like those of a eunuch (śamanīcāmeḍhra)—if they were to reach the *nidhana* [of the chant] as prescribed by the etymological explanation (*nirukta*), then the householder alone would depart, having failed; "whose Brāhmaṇa-explanation would this be? ask the teachers.
They say it is a prohibition against the *naudhasa* [sāman]. 12–14.

Because its finale (*nidhana*) is etymologically derived [from *indra*], they call it "Indra" as the finale in the *dyautāna* [chant]; there is a prohibition against that, and they should approach it exactly according to the traditional recitation (*āmnāya*).
And regarding the turban and the goad: the turban which is tied crosswise belongs to those who are not *vrātyas*.
The Vrātyas go along, being driven by a bow that has no arrow;
their quiver is strung, and their path is a wrong road strewn with wooden planks—thus says Śāṇḍilya, that the chariot should be yoked with a trembling horse and a mule.
Dhānañjayya says it may be with any two horses or any two mules whatsoever.
Thus ends the first section in the twenty-third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. Regarding the garment: "A black garment," says Śāṇḍilya, meaning one mixed with *kadru* (mottled) fibers.
"A white garment with a black border," says Gautama.
Dhānañjayya says that one should consider [the skin] as simply "black.
(3) [The phrase is] "on a black-and-white antelope skin.
(4) If each of the two [skins] were purchased with two sheep, then those two antelope skins should be joined along their sides, being black on one side and white on the other. (5)
"Valakṣa" means white; "rajato niṣkaḥ" refers to a silver coin; all this, including the phrase "that of the householder," the householder should provide.
And thirty-three [coins]. 6–8.
Dhānañjayya says there should be two or three sets of thirty-three. The fringes and tassels should be made of wool; for the others, the garments should be woven with red woollen threads.
Regarding "with fringes and tassels," they should have fringes at the ends of the threads.

The one called *daśākhyā* is *tūṣa*, according to Śāṇḍilya; "two by two are the leather straps," "two by two are the sandals," and "black with ear-ornaments" [are the shoes], according to Dhānaṃjayya; "whatever [shoes there are]," according to Dhānaṃjayya. 14.
"The skins are joined in pairs" has been explained by the two preceding [rules regarding] skins (15).
"One of the others should fetch each one" (16),
and "thirty-three" (17).
Eighteen: "Thirty-three householders shall assemble for each [of the thirty-three].
Nineteen: "They shall give thirty-three [cows] to the officiating priests.
Twenty: "The wealth of those who have become *vrātyas*—those who have not desisted from the *vrātya* way of life—shall be given to other *vrātyas*, or to a Brahmin from the Magadha country."

Because they cleanse themselves in that very person from whom they receive this [gift], (21) having sacrificed with them, they should maintain the livelihood of those learned in the three Vedas. (22) He may eat after them and he should officiate as their priest. (23)
Thus ends the second section in the twenty-third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra. 2. There are six Agniṣṭuts. 1.
The first two are Trivṛt Jyotiṣṭomas, with the Svarṣāma and Vāravantīya [stotras], because of the diversity of the desires for the respective offices. 2.
Or rather, it is not so, because there is no distinction regarding the *trivṛt* [stoma] (3),
because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the *vāravantīya* [sāman] to the subsequent [verses] (4),
and because of the plurality of recitations (*anuvāka*) in the sacrifices (5).
The teachers say there are four [additional days] because of the traditional recitation;
because of the repeated mention, they belong to both the Trivṛt and the Jyotiṣṭoma;
and for all [the days], the first Anuvāka is identical, as in the case of the Gavāmayana.

There is no distinctness of sacrificial rites (*kratu*) due to the diversity of the *anuvākas*, as in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma* with respect to the *anuvākas*; and as in the cases of the *cāturmāsya*, *vājapeya*, *rājasūya*, and *garga-trirātra*. In these [rites], one should give oxen, horses, and goats according to one's capacity; likewise for gold. Whoever, being worthy of some object, does not obtain it, he should sacrifice with the first *trivṛt* [stoma]. For that [sacrifice], a chariot drawn by four horses is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and among them, one should be dark-brown (*śyāva*).
He whom the Brahmins together with the kings might honor should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava.
At his morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts.
He should not withhold them from the officiating priests.
At the midday pressing, there are twelve horses;
he removes them both [from the sacrificial post] at that time.
At the third pressing, there are eleven; he should remove them once the omentum of the *anūbandhya* victim has been offered. These [horses] should also be eleven hundred each, or perhaps thousands.
The horse is permanent at midday.
(18) Those who would thus place him first should thereafter conduct themselves toward them as one who has become subordinate. (19) And they should call him "the master builder" (*sthapati*). (20)
The *iṣu* sacrifice is explained by [the rules for] the *śyena*.
However, its *dīkṣā* and *upasad* rites are those of the one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice.
Thus ends the third section in the twenty-third chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 3.21–22.3.

One who is about to sacrifice with the *sarvasvāra* should strive from the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) onwards so that he may pass away on the day of the Soma-pressing (*sautya*). 1. He should consume the *prāṇabhakṣa* (breath-consumptions) as the regular portions at all times.
2. He should cause those [portions] to be swallowed by water, or he should pour them over himself. 3.
Having mixed the *soma* with water, they should pour it out at the place where the *mārjālīya* fire is located.

While the *ārbhava-pavamāna* chant is being sung, he should spread a black antelope skin to the south of the *audumbarī* post and lie down covered, with his head toward the south. "In that very way one comes together; in that very way one dies"—thus [it is said].
Having cast this deceased sacrificer into the *āhavanīya* fire along with the oblations, the *rjīṣa*, and the sacrificial vessels, they should depart—so says Śāṇḍilya.
Dhānañjayya says that they should complete the remainder [of the ritual].
Śāṇḍilyāyana Nediṣṭhin says that if they should complete it, then, having fastened that black antelope skin, the sacrificer should perform the duties of the patron and consume the portions.
Dhānañjayya says that the officiating priests should perform the duties of the patron and offer all the oblations as consumptions.
When the day has ended, they should collect the parts of the throne with the verse, "May they strengthen thee" (RV 3.8.4).
They should wash them with the verse, "May they cleanse thee" (RV 3.8.5). They should carve them with the verse, "They have carved thee" (RV 3.8.6).
They should separate [the sacrificer] with the words, "Be peaceful, O pacifiers.

Having led him to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and covered him with the Soma-wrapper, they should have his hair and beard shaved at the southern edge of the altar after the omentum of the Anūbandhya animal has been offered.
Having completed the remainder of the Anūbandhya rite, they should pile up the funeral mound (citā) in the middle of the sacrificial ground.
The Āhavanīya fire is in the east, the Gārhapatya fire in the west, the Anvāhāryapacana fire to the south, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire to the west of the Gārhapatya, and the body in the middle.
(16) The Adhvaryu should arrange that [body], placed upon the altar with its head toward the south, using the sacrificial vessels. (17) He should place the potsherds on the head. (18)
The *samoptadhāna* vessel on the forehead, the *prāśitraharaṇa* on the [forehead],
and the two *sruva* spoons on the two nostrils. 16, 20, 21.
Having placed gold in the mouth and having covered the face with the omentum of the cow used for the funeral pyre, he places the *āgnihotra-havanī* ladle across there;
the *juhū* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left.
On the two sides, the *spaye* (25); likewise, the *vṛkvaus* (26); on the chest, the *dhuvām* (27).
The bowl on the belly (28),
the black antelope skin on the lap (26),
and between the thighs the *śamyā* and the *dṛṣad-upala* stones (29); and whatever else we shall not specify (30).
To the south of the southern hearth (ukha), the mortar (ulūkhala) is placed; 31. along the thigh, the pestle (musala); 32.
at the two feet, the cart and the winnowing basket (śūrpa). 33.

Having made all [the vessels] turned face upwards, with pouring-spouts, and containing speckled butter, they should spread out a row of *ulapa* grass for all the fires so that the fires may meet within it. 34. If it should go out first from the Āhavanīya fire, one should know: "He will go to the world of Brahman. From the Gārhapatya fire: "To the world of the gods. From the Dakṣiṇāgni fire: "To the world of the ancestors. 35.
Thus, when he has been prepared with the sacrificial vessels, the Sāmavedin should chant over him the verse: "The eagle on the firmament... 36.
When smoke has arisen, he should recite "O brilliant one, this is your smoke" (RV 10.162.2) and "The smoke rises up" (RV 10.162.3).
When it has burst into flames, he should recite either of these two verses beginning with "O Agni, be gracious" (RV 4.1.4) and "Thou art great" (RV 4.1.5).
In that same manner, elderly Vedic scholars sing around the known [fire], thinking: "This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, shall go to the heavenly world. Thus one should know.
If he should live, he should sacrifice with the *udavasānīyā* offering (40).
"Thereafter, he should seek death by fasting," says Śāṇḍilya (41). "He should eat if he wishes to live," says Dhānañjayya (42).
Cooked food is the sacrificial fee for that [rite].
43 One should commence the Cāturmāsya sacrifices on the full moon day of Phālguna. 44 The interval of time has been stated by the Brāhmaṇa. 45

On the day of sacrifice, there should be the Vaiśvadeva and the Śunāsīrya offerings; and the northern [portion] of the Vāruṇapraghāsika. On the full-moon day, the last of the Sākamedha offerings [is performed]. One hundred and twelve cows are the sacrificial fee for the Śunāsīrya.
"For each of the other fifty days, [the procedure is] one by one," thus says Drāhyāyaṇa in the fourth section of the twenty-third chapter of the Śrautasūtra. 4.
In the Upahavya sacrifice, they should pronounce the names of the deities indirectly in their respective places. 1.
1. They should avoid the word "deva" (god) everywhere when [the deities] are in their improper places.

2–3. The Hotṛ should recite these two [verses]: "The god Hotṛ... and "The great [sacrifice] of Mitra..."; instead, he should say "The Hotṛ [is] the sacrifice" and "The great [sacrifice] of the sacrifice. 4.
The sacrificial fee prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa is "the moon," that is, Soma;
one should give something to the others as well.

For the Ṛtapeya sacrifice, there are twelve initiation days and upasad days; thus, there are three upasads, or six. "He becomes one whose vow is ghee"—he should consume it during the initiation days according to his capacity. "He approaches with each successive section"—Śāṇḍilya says that he should consume it separately during the upasads using the finger-joints in reverse order.

All the *camasa* vessels should be measured by the separate joints of a single finger. Regarding this, Śaucivṛkṣi says they should be measured with the fingers pointing in the natural direction (*anuloma*), while Dhānañjayya says they should be measured with the fingers pointing in the reverse direction (*pratiloma*).

Having uttered "Ṛta," those who are about to enter the *sadas* and those who are about to consume the portions should say "O God, speak the truths! and having said "This is the earth," they should say "Yonder sun shall rise in the morning."
Dhānañjayya maintains that those deities for whom the cups are offered should modify the consumption mantras to reflect that they have drunk from them;
however, there is no modification for the Nārāśaṃsa cups.
Some teachers hold this same view regarding all sacrifices.
And they arrange the food and the *chandas* verses;
17. the teachers [perform this] everywhere without modification. 18. "A *soma*-cup is the sacrificial fee"—this should apply to the pressed [Soma]. 19.
For in that [case], the measure is the cup (camasa).
At midday, they should pour it out together with those who hold the cups at the front;
and when it has been offered, it should be given away—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), without carrying it out to the east of the Āhavanīya fire, they should have the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds carried around by the south of the Vedi; then they should enter the Sadas by the eastern door.
When the day's rite has concluded, one should give something to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Thus ends the first section of the twenty-fourth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa for the Dūṇāśa sacrifice as follows:
1. "As many [units] as there are two hundred and twenty-eight *mānas* [of gold], where there might be twenty-four *mānas*, one should give that many two hundred and twenty-eights.
2. "A golden disk (*rukma*) for the Hotṛ"—this refers to an ornament called a *niṣka*; one should give that. 3. "A garland (*sraj*) for the Udgātṛ"—it should be made of gold.

In the Vaiśyastoma, they should mix Soma with milk that has been freshly milked at the morning pressing, with boiled milk at the midday pressing, and with curds at the third pressing. Its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are either one hundred and twelve or a thousand, according to the prescribed forms. In the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice, animals are immolated.

Regarding the Tīvrasut sacrifice, one should cause him who has been purified by Soma to sacrifice; Śāṇḍilya says that he who becomes worse after having sacrificed is one who has been purified by Soma (somātipavita).

Dhānañjayya says that one who, having drunk the Soma, should vomit or purge [should perform this]. Or, as some say, the eldest sacrificer may be without a share while the younger ones have shares. In that case, they should smell the cups according to the ritual procedure for consuming (bhakṣāvṛt).
"The officiating priests do not consume [the soma], but merely smell the cups," so it is said.

They should consume them during the *acchāvāka*'s hymn; thus it is for all the pressings. Regarding the statement, "They pour out [more] soma over and over again," they should pour out more only over those [cups] which they have smelled.
"Let them milk a hundred [cows] with the *āśira* mixture": having caused a hundred cows to be milked, they should divide that into three parts and mix it with Soma, as in the *vaiśyastoma*.

Its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is that same hundred cows; for he says, "Those indeed are the sacrificial fees. Thus ends the second section in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 2.2.14–15.
He whom Brahmins and kings might place at their head should perform the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having undergone initiation on the full moon day, he should undergo thirteen initiations,
or seventeen.
Gautama says that one should undergo initiation on the new moon day for a month;
Dhānañjayya says for a year;
and [the view is] that it should be a rite with six *upasad* days and involving the piling of the fire-altar.

Having arranged the *pārṣṭika* stomas within the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, one should sacrifice for a year during the bright fortnights (*pūrvapakṣa*) with those [stomas] which are excluded from the Jyotiṣṭoma and begin with that [first day]. (7) Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya on the thirteenth bright fortnight, one should perform the other year with these same [stomas] repeated. (8) These [sacrifices] should have sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's capacity. (9)
"Lāmakāyana says that one should sacrifice with the Rājasūya;
the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa [stomas] should take the place of the Abhyārohaṇīya, and the Vājapeya should take the place of the Abhiṣecanīya. (10–12)
The fifteenth [day] is the *trivṛt* of the *keśavapanīya*. 13.
The *jyotiṣṭoma* is for the *vyuṣṭi* and *kṣatradhṛti* [sacrifices]. 14.
One should perform the *bṛhaspatisava* both before and after [the main sacrifice], says Śāṇḍilya. 15.
Dhānañjayya says that one should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma for a month before [the sacrifice] and likewise after it;
Gautama says that one should finally perform only the Pratyavarohaṇīya sacrifice, and not any of these others. One should choose seventeen priests, including the Sadasya, as distinct officiants.

His sacrificial fee consists of female slaves, gold ornaments, chariots, elephant-vehicles, and cattle; for each one of these types born [in his possession], there are seventeen thousand, or seventeen hundred, or even just seventeen cows.
This is what they call the Kuru-Vājapeya.
He should distribute those [objects] equally among the officiating priests (ṛtvij),

or he may give the best portion to the central performers. He should give the chariot with which he ran the race to the Udgātṛ, as well as the throne-seat (āsandī) with its coverlet, upon which he, when consecrated, would mount.
A goat-skin with gold [ornaments] for the Hotṛ, on which he shall sit while being consecrated;
(25) a girdle made of cloth for the Adhvaryu; (26) a golden bowl filled with honey for the Brahman; (27)
Or he may offer grains of parched rice mixed with honey in a bronze vessel.
(28) Thus ends the third section in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. His observances are as follows: (1)
He should follow the occupation of a Kṣatriya.
He should avoid descending [from his seat], saluting, walking behind [a superior], and sharing a bed with those who have not performed the Vājapeya sacrifice;
however, he may do so according to age with those who have performed the Vājapeya sacrifice.
"Having performed the Pratyavarohaṇīya sacrifice, one should not observe these vows," says Śāṇḍilyāyana. There are alternatives for this:

either the Vājapeya is performed according to its original form, or one should arrange the Stomas beginning with the Ekaviṃśa and increasing by two up to the Saptadaśa and Trayastriṃśa; that is the "Mayūra" (Peacock) arrangement, not the "Ekarṣi."
For him, the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is "Sing forth for him, O men" (*tasyopāsmai gāyatā naraḥ*).
Regarding this, Śāṇḍilya says that by means of this very *brahmasāman*, one ascends to the heavenly world.
Alternatively, it is the *jyotiṣṭoma* *atirātra* sacrifice without the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Or it may be an *anatirātra* sacrifice with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup;
for that, the *stotra* should have the *bṛhat* chant with the seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*) hymn-form, while its own verses should have the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*) hymn-form.
Or it may be an *agniṣṭoma*.

For that [sacrifice], one should arrange the *abhīvarta* as the *brahmasāman* on an *anuṣṭubh* verse, and the *yajñāyajñīya* as the *agniṣṭomasāman*. The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], and the *pañcaviṃśa-stoma* is the *brahmasāman*; or else, the *caturviṃśa-stoma* is the *acchāvākasāman*, and the other [laud] is the same.
Or rather, for this [sacrifice], the *pṛṣṭha* lauds are in the *catustriṃśa-stoma*, and the *agniṣṭomasāman* is the *saptadaśa-stoma*, while everything else remains the same.
Gautama says that none of these [options] constitute a true *vājapeya*.
And the sacrificer should not give the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of the *vājapeya* at these [rites]; he should give them, he should give them. 17.
Thus ends the fourth section in the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. 4.
A king should sacrifice with the *rājasūya*. 1.

On the first day of the fortnight of Phālguna, one should undergo initiation for the Abhyārohaṇīya Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. For that, there is one period of initiation and one hundred and twelve cows as the sacrificial fee.
After a year has passed, one should perform the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice.
His initiation is exactly like that. Gautama says there are two [days] for the Abhyārohaṇīya;
Śāṇḍilya says there is one day for the Abhyārohaṇīya and three days for the Abhiṣecanīya.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, however, he should undergo initiation.
For this sacrifice, he should give thirty-two thousand [cows] as sacrificial fees; he should give them to the *madhyataḥkārin* priests, one thousand to each.
To the *prastotṛ*, *maitrāvaruṇa*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, and *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, he should give sixteen [each], which is half of that amount.
Eight [cows] are for the Pratihartṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka; these are the third-part recipients (tṛtīyinyaḥ). 11.
Four are for the Subrahmaṇya, Agnīdhra, Unnetṛ, and Grāvastut; these are the quarter-part recipients (pādinyaḥ). 12.
One should cause the kinsmen of the Abalāna, who are well-provided for, to carry them away, and one should win them over at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇāvelāyām). 13.
And he should shoot arrows at them; they themselves should bring those back, saying, "Be victorious, O King!
He should give a third of their wealth to the officiating priests.

At the Daśapeya sacrifice, one should give the third [portion] to those who have entered [the sacrificial ground]; 17. one should return the remainder to them alone; 18. one should also give [portions] to the village people. 19.

Those who are Kṣatriyas shall be his [officiants] from that point onward, but they are not to be consecrated. Having performed that sacrifice, he should not personally descend for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). He should deposit either a black antelope horn or the foot of a black antelope skin.
From this point, he should go out wearing sandals made of boar-skin, and return wearing those made of black antelope skin.
Thus ends the first section of the twenty-fifth chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
He who has been initiated for that [sacrifice] should sacrifice with the Daśapeya on the tenth day.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa says: "Ten by ten they approach the cup. They should consume the Udgātṛ's cup in four groups of three, and the others in six groups of two.
In this manner, for each of the others, they should proceed until ten are completed from the vessels other than that of the sacrificer.
Having recited, "Ten mothers, ten fathers," they should move forward as far as the tenth person, for so it is said.
Wherever they might encounter a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, they should complete that number of ten with a Brāhmaṇa woman alone.
And so that they may remember what they have not yet remembered, they should stand near the hearths together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
A garland is for the Udgātṛ; he who is about to bathe for the Bahiṣpavamāna should fasten upon him a golden garland with three lotuses.
When the sacrificer is seated in the *āstāva*, he should offer a water-vessel with twelve lotuses belonging to the sacrificer himself.
(9) When the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, he should return the water-vessel to the sacrificer. (10) By means of the other release, he should perform the entire day’s rite. (11)
He himself should take that [fee].
(12) "The two *prākāśa* vessels belong to the two *adhvaryu*s": the golden one should be on the right side for the *adhvaryu*, and the silver one on the left side for the *pratiprasthātṛ*.
(13) "The garment belongs to the *potṛ*": it should be made of cotton. (14)

The sacrificial sword of the Neṣṭṛ should be made of linen; the others are known to be made of wool by the Brāhmaṇa [text]. Having emerged from its purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he should observe the Devavrata vow for one year.
He should run about without treading upon anything and without bathing (18). He should gnaw his teeth, clip his nails, and shave his beard, but not his hair (19).
He should lie down on a tiger skin with the hair facing upward in the fire-hall (20).
Day by day he should place fuel on the fire; 21.
He should not enter a village; 24. No non-Brahmins should cause him to sow seeds in his kingdom. 23.
And one should not clip the hair of horses; nor their teeth; nor their hooves. 24–26.
"But the Brāhmaṇas may do as they intend, as well as those who follow them.

(27) Thus ends the second section in the twenty-fifth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. After one year has passed, he should undergo initiation for the Keśavapanīya sacrifice at the same time that he would perform the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice. (1)
For him, there is an Atirātra on the full-moon day;
having sacrificed with the Daśapeya, Dhānañjayya says that he should sacrifice with the Keśavapanīya during the subsequent fortnight of the waxing moon,
and the Atirātra likewise takes place on the full-moon day.

A thousand is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having performed the Udavasānīyā offering for that, one should undergo initiation for the Vyaṣṭidvirātra sacrifice by means of the Paurṇamāsa [offering]. If one intends to perform it on the new moon day, the first day [of the rite] should be on the new moon;
if on the full moon day, one should undergo initiation during the bright fortnight itself.
Of the two [types of] *vicāra* sacrifices, the subsequent day is to be offered;
regarding the *vyaṣṭakā*, it is the subsequent one—these are called the first three *vyaṣṭakās* of the dark fortnight (*tāmisra*).
Both should indeed take place in the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), for he says: "Those which belong to the same fortnight."

The southern [altar] has been explained by [the description of] the eastern one. (11) One should sacrifice with the Kṣatradhṛti [offering] during that same first fortnight, if there should be an opportunity. (12) If it is not available, then during the next first fortnight. (13)
That [sacrifice] is explained by the Abhyārohaṇīya.
Regarding those two, Gautama and Dhānañjayya say that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of one thousand [cows] for each.
And at the Keśavapanīya, there are two thousand.
Likewise, there are four [gifts] at the Vyuṣṭi sacrifice; Gautama says there are four at the Abhiṣecanīya, while Dhānaṃjayya says there are five;
however, the wealth of one's weak kinsmen is always [to be given].

One should give twenty-one groups according to one's enthusiasm; one should sacrifice with the *ṛṣabha* [offering] belonging to Indra both before and after [the main rites]. A king desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with this.
In the Virāj [chant], one should offer ten groups according to one's enthusiasm (23).
One should perform the circumferential offerings with an animal dedicated to Agni both before and after (24). With the Vaiśvadeva [offering], there is the upaśada (25).
Its sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twenty-four [cows] (26).
Having caused them to sacrifice or initiate them during their youth—both the superior and the inferior—he, upon returning home from his studies, should perform the *Punaḥstoma* sacrifice (27).
Its sacrificial fee consists of twelve pairs, according to Dhānañjayya (28).
"Furthermore, a refurbished chariot, a mended skin of a black antelope, a milch cow, and a calf—these, says Śāṇḍilya;
one should give these according to one's means.
In the case of the two Catuṣṭoma sacrifices involving single-hoofed animals, one should give according to one's means in the former."
"In both cases, [the offering is] on the subsequent day," according to Drāhyāyaṇa’s Śrautasūtra, Chapter Twenty-five, Section Three. 3.
One should sacrifice with the Udbhid and Balabhid [sāmans] without separating them. 1.
Both of these would have seven endings;
2. it would occur within half a month in the spring;
3. [or] a month; 4. or a year.
In that regard, there is the iṣu-iṣṭi sacrifice (5).
For those two, there are two chariots yoked with four horses each, covered with skins, and equipped on both sides with bronze armor (7).
The horses should be of the *śatārhā* breed, or capable of performing a hundred actions (8).
"A king should sacrifice with these two," says Śāṇḍilya; "anyone who desires honor," says Dhānañjayya. The means for the Agni-stomas has been stated by means of the one-day vow.
For those two, the sacrificial fees consist of four separate heaps of grain;
in the eastern [fire] there are six oxen, and in the northern [fire] there are four oxen. The sacrificial fee consists of twelve hundred bulls, with one thousand [cows] for the *varṣabha* bull.
Among those that are not present, some may be bulls, others may be castrated males, and others may be young steers.
That Vaiśya whom the people, together with the king, should elect, he shall sacrifice with the Gosava. This is explained by the Bṛhaspatisava;
however, its sacrificial fee is ten thousand.

Those who are friends or brothers who may accomplish [the rite] together should sacrifice with the Marutstoma. 18. Its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are of appropriate form; at the Pañcaśāradīya, offspring are offered as victims. They should give of these according to their means. 19.
"Of whichever [of the participants]," says Dhānañjayya. 20.

The family-offering belongs to Indra and Agni; the nest-rite consists of one thousand [oblations] at the Indra-stoma. The king and the domestic priest should perform a sacrifice with the Indra-Agni stoma.

A Brāhmaṇa should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of the Gāyatrī, while a King should give one consisting of the Jagatī. (24) They may, however, perform the sacrifice separately according to their desire. (25) In that case, the sacrificial fees for those two remain exactly as described. (26)
One desiring cattle, or one practicing sorcery, should sacrifice with the two Vighana [hymns].
(27) One should employ the Atharvaṇa Sāman known as Somasāman in the sacrifice of one desiring cattle; one practicing sorcery should employ the Somasāman.
(28) The sacrificial fees for one desiring cattle should consist of Bṛhatī verses. (29)
The [rites] for one practicing malevolent magic with an arrow have been explained;
so too those involving the *saṃdaṃśa* and the *vajra*.
One should practice malevolent magic against a king with the *saṃdaṃśa*, and against a kingdom with the *vajra*.
One performing malevolent magic against a king should employ these two [sacrifices] in reverse order.
Finally, one should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma for the sake of pacification—for the sake of pacification.
Thus ends the fourth section in the twenty-fifth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
The Ahīna sacrifices conclude with the month of the initiation for the Paurṇamāsī;
they have twelve Upasad days, or six, according to Dhānaṃjayya. The tail of the sacrifice occurs on the twenty-first day or the thirtieth.

In the case of an excess of truth, there is a reduction of the initiation (dīkṣā). 4. All Atirātra sacrifices are Ahīna sacrifices, as are the multi-day sessions (ahargaṇa) beginning with the Dvirātra, 5.
except for the Cāturmāsya and the Rājasūya. 6.

Because of the interruption of the *Ṛgveda* and *Sāmaveda* recitations, and because of their difference from the *Ahīna* sacrifices, there is a distinction for them regarding the night: "Panyaṃ panyaṃ," "Śrautakakṣaṃ," "Daivodāsaṃ," "Hotṛṣāma," "Kautsasya loke," "Āṣṭādaṃṣṭraṃ," and "Tvāmāviśantu.
Other than the Aśvamedha, those [sacrifices] which have a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) precede the four-night (*catūrātra*) rites.
From that point onward, there are many more [soma] pressings due to the accumulation of offerings:

according to some, based on the view of the established doctrine (*kṛtānta*), they amount to thirty-three hundred and three; according to another view, one hundred and twenty-five thousand are produced during the three-night rite (*trirātra*).
Thus is the attainment of ten thousand [cows] in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice (13).
One should distribute them equally over all the days (14). In the case of an equal attainment [of cows], the greatest number should be given on the final day (15).
One should give eleven ten-thousands on the eleventh night; nine hundred on each of the preceding days, and one thousand on the final day.
On the first day of the three-night periods, one should give to those who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call and to the *grāvastut* priest; and on the final day, to the *chandoga* singers.
The middle [share] is for the others;
one should give one hundred to each of those who perform the work from the center,
fifty to the half-sharers.
Twenty for the *potr̥* from the third group, thirty for the *neṣṭr̥*, and [thirty] each for the other two; 22.
And for the *āgnīdhra*; 23.
Nine for the *unnetr̥* from the fourth group, ten for the other two; 24.

"One should give equally to the Unnetṛ every day," thus says the first section of the twenty-sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra. Ten [cows] to the Sadasya on the first day, seventy on the second, and twenty on the third.
Ten [cows] are to be given to those who claim descent from ten ancestors, as stated by the Brāhmaṇa;

two who have studied the Vedas (anūcānau) on the first two days, and one who has not studied them (ananūcāna) on the last day. Ten hundred cows are left over; he should give them either to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) or to the attendants (prasarpaka).
The thousandth [part], the sixteenth digit, on the middle day is for Brahman and the Āgnīdhra.
White, black, and red are its forms. Ten digits are for Brahman; five for the Āgnīdhra.

One should make [the cow] desireless; having ransomed her with another cow and having given permission with the words "She is for a specific desire," one should mutter [the mantra] into her right ear and release her among the cows.
Because it is taught immediately following the Jyotiṣṭoma procedure, it should be an integral part of the Dvādaśāha sacrifice.
And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga), as in the case of the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
and because of repeated recitation, as in the case of the *ahīna* and *ekāha* sacrifices;
and because, like various sections, there would be no connection between those enjoined merely by proximity, as in the case of the *upahavya* and *rājasūya*.

The mention of the *liṅga* (indicative mark) is for another purpose, as in the case of the *śakvarī* verses on the sixth day [of the *Ṣaḍaha*]. Furthermore, the restatement is a rule regarding the remainder (*śeṣavidhi*).
In that independent [rite], there should be the *Ahīnarātri*, for it is enjoined without distinction among the *Ahīna* sacrifices.
It should indeed be the natural one, because it is prescribed as the subject matter;
there is no specific injunction regarding the remainder, just as in the case of the fourfold cutting.
By this, the substitution for the *oṃ* syllable with speech in the *rathantara* has been explained.
And because the meaning of the word is impossible [in that context],
there is a conjunction of those two like the apaghāṭilā plant;
the statement "speech is to be taken" is merely a reversal of the location.
As in the case of the Vāmadevya and Yajñāyajñīya [sāmans].
Thus ends the second section in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 2.
In the Aptoryāma sacrifice, the embryos are performed according to the ritual procedure (kalpa). 1.
Either the Rathantara is the *pṛṣṭha* chant, or in its place is the Bārhatam Vājijit; the Bṛhat and the Vāravantīya are the two subsequent *pṛṣṭhas*;
and the Vāravantīya is performed upon the verses of the Kāleya.
In its place, first [the hymn] of Samanta (5),
then that of Kāleya (6) for Pārtha, and that of Uśanas (7);
these very same [hymns] are on the backs (7).
Dhānañjayya says that one should place the Vaiśvajita Ājya-stotras in the Ājya-stotras and the Ṣāṣṭhika Uktha-stotras in the Uktha-stotras.
Śāṇḍilya says this according to the rule of the Ṛṣis.
Or rather, in the Jyotiṣṭoma Atirātra, one should add the extra stotras of the Ṣoḍaśin.
Those very same *garbha* [stotras] are on the back days (*pṛṣṭha*), and the *Yajñāyajñīya* is the *Bṛhat-garbha*.
(11) At the *Ekastoma* sacrifices and at the *Vaida-trirātra*, there should be an *Atirātra* with its own *stomas*; likewise for the *saṃdhi*. (12) For both proceed without modification. (13)
Furthermore, the state of being "turned away" (parāktva) for the *trivṛt* [stoma] is not possible except at the junction (*saṃdhi*).

(14) The injunction "with the *trivṛt* *atirātra*" is a general prescription (*aviśeṣacodanā*). (15) And there is no requirement for repetition (*vṛtti*) in the case of a specific instruction (*ādeśa*), as in: "The first night-sacrifice has sixteen [verses]. (16)
Regarding that, some teachers say that even in the *baidottama* [recitation], it is "intermediate" (madhyama). 17.

Insertion (*āvāpa*) or repetition (*abhyāsa*) is stated in the sense of the *saṃdhi*. 18. Or it is according to the *Anubrāhmaṇa*; because of the connection with the original form (*prakṛti*), they are twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśāḥ*). 19.
But it is without a *stoma*, because of the context;
nor does it occur in a single [verse],
for it would be improper that the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) [stoma] should be greater than the *ukthas*.
"May it be accomplished," says Śocivṛkṣi (23).
The Ekaviṃśa and Pañcadaśa are the *stomas* for the two middle days, while the others are for the other two (24).
"Having placed the fire near the Brāhmaṇas who chant the Ājyadohas, they sing praises," so it is said (25).
They should maintain the fire at the Hotṛ’s hearth; that which they would bring at midday on the first day,
they should kindle it at the time of the Stotra during the morning pressing on the two subsequent days.
Thus ends the third section in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.
One who desires a thousandfold prosperity should perform the Śabalī-homa;
however, Dhānañjayya maintains that one who has performed the three-night sacrifice (Agnihotra) should not do so.
"Indeed, it says: 'He causes this [cow] to be given for three nights';
Śāṇḍilya says this applies to anyone who desires a thousandfold prosperity. It says: 'One who, being capable of eating food, does not eat food.'"

In the spring, on the first day of the waxing fortnight, having had his hair and beard shaved and having put on a new garment, he should drink boiled milk for twelve nights; he should sleep on the ground on an uncovered surface. His fire, constantly maintained, should be kept in his dwelling.
No other friend acting as an attendant should enter after him.
He should speak little (6) and not go far (10).

On the twelfth day, at dawn, having swept around the fire and strewn grass around it, there should be a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood, as well as a *sruk* and a *sruva* ladle, and likewise a *camasa* cup. Having poured together curds, honey, and clarified butter into that cup, he should take [the mixture] into the *sruk* with the *sruva*; here he should offer it either four times or eight times, with the mantra: "Thou art the speckled ocean" (11).
With the utterance of *svāhā*, he offers the northern portion (12).
Whatever remains in the *sruk* spoon, having poured that into the *camasa* cup, he should consume it (13).
Having washed the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, he should set them down along with the *camasa* cup (14).
"Into that very place he should cast [the offering]," says Śāṇḍilyāyana.

(15) Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having proceeded to a forest where one cannot hear the sound of domestic cattle, and having touched a clump of darbha grass there, he should cry out three times with his full voice, "Śabalī! Śabalī!
(16) If someone other than a dog or a donkey should bark in response, he should know that the rite has been successful. (17)
In this manner, one should perform the practice for up to three years without being answered by the barking of a dog.

If, however, at the very beginning a dog or a donkey should bark in response, one should know that there is no hope for cattle. But if it does not bark in response for up to three years, there is hope for cattle.
"Peace! The Vāmadevya hymn! Peace! The Vāmadevya hymn! (21).
Thus ends the fourth section in the twenty-sixth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 4.
A king who is unassailable should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. 1.
The means for that [is as follows]: according to the Gautamīya [tradition] in the Mahāvrata, there are daily *upasad* rites; having been initiated, one should release a white horse.
The black circle of the eye is its form (5). Those who are endowed with speed (6),
not turning back from the quarters, having protected it for a year, should bind it at the purchase of the King (Soma) (7).

Dhānañjayya says that one should begin in the summer; Śāṇḍilya says in the spring. On the seventh or eighth day of either Caitra or Vaiśākha, having fed the priests who perform the central rites with *brahmaudana*, one should give them separate gifts of a thousand [cows] each.
When the sacrifice to Pūṣan has been commenced or completed, one should set the horse free.

In that regard, there are three *iṣṭi* offerings dedicated to Savitṛ. When these have been completed, the sacrificer and likewise the Hotṛ sit facing east upon golden cushions to the south of the Āhavanīya fire. For one year, day after day, he should listen to the Hotṛ as he recites the *pāriplava* narrative.
To the east, the Adhvaryu sits facing west on two golden planks with a golden cushion between them; the Brahman and the Udgātṛ sit facing north.
He should give a hundred [cows] to the Hotṛ, ten to the Adhvaryu, or a thousand to the Hotṛ and a hundred to the Adhvaryu.
Some [rites] are performed with the other two [fires]. 18.
His divine vows are as in the Rājasūya. 19.
After one year has passed, he should bind the horse and undergo initiation. 20.

On that day, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should take their respective seats. There are twelve initiation days (dīkṣā) for him, as well as twelve preparatory days (upasad). For all the days, they should chant the Bahiṣpavamāna hymn outside the sacrificial hall.

Thus ends the first section of the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Drāhyāyaṇa-Śrautasūtra*. On the middle day, having touched the tail-hair of the horse, they should proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
While they are proceeding, the sacrificer should say to the *udgātṛ*: "O *udgātṛ*, I choose you with a hundred *niṣkas*; my horse shall sing the *udgītha*."
Having made the horse step onto the *āstāva* (the place of chanting), they should show it to him.
When it neighs toward it, then the sacrificer should say to the *udgātṛ*: "O *udgātṛ*, I choose you with a hundred [coins] and with a *niṣka*; you alone shall chant for me as the *udgātṛ*.

Having made the horse step out toward the north and having sat down on the *āstāva*, the *udgātṛ* should chant the praise with the three-verse hymn beginning, "The vigorous steed, omniform... (*abhivājī viśvarūpa*).
Seated upon the *hiraṇyakaśipu*, having praised with the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, he himself shall carry that [water].
Or, whichever wife of the sacrificer is most beloved, she may carry it. A princess who has not been honored is called a *parivṛktī*.
When the sacrificial animals have been designated and the Hotṛ has made his advances, the Brahman should likewise make advances toward her.
[He should say: "Lift her up, as one carrying a load upon a mountain; let her middle swell, as the cold wind blows again. He should point this out.

One hundred daughters of Rājanyas should be her attendants. They should make advances toward him: "Lift him up, as one carrying a load upon a mountain; let his middle be like lac in the cold wind. They should point this out.
The Udgātṛ should mock the Parivṛktī, pointing her out with the words: "What they have made of her thighs—broad and well-seated, her testicles quiver like two insects in a cow's hoof-print.

(12) Her hundred female attendants—the daughters of charioteers and village headmen—should mock him in return, pointing him out with the words: "O gods, that which they have revealed as a limp-limbed, deformed thing.
(13) "The woman points with her thigh, just as the eye of truth moves. (14)
Having touched water and sung the Vāmadevya hymn, they should recite the verses of that [hymn] after it.
Thus ends the second section of the twenty-seventh chapter in the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra.
When the offerings with the *svāhākṛti* formulas have been performed, they should sit down to the east of the *sadas* and engage in the theological debate (*brahmodya*). 1.

When the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu have spoken, the Brahman shall ask the Udgātṛ: "I ask you for the sake of knowledge, O friend of the gods: do you know by your mind that upon which Viṣṇu rested in his three steps, and into which the entire world has entered?
He should answer him: "Even upon those three steps into which the entire world has entered, I instantly encompass both the earth and the sky with a single limb—the back of this heaven."

The Udgātṛ should ask the Brahman: "What indeed has entered within the person? What things are deposited within the person? This we ask you, O Brahman; what shall I answer you here? (4) He should reply to him: "Five things have entered within the person; these things are deposited within the person. Reflecting upon this for you here, you become superior through your creative power (*māyā*) in this Aditi. (5) All [the priests] should ask the sacrificer: "We ask you about the seed of the virile horse; we ask about the highest heaven of speech. (6)

He should say to them: "This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world; this Soma is the seed of the virile horse; this Brahman is the highest heaven of speech. (7) On the first day he should give a thousand as sacrificial fees, and likewise on the last day.
(8) On the middle day, he should give whatever wealth belongs to non-Brahmins within a single district. (9)
Or he should sacrifice in the middle of his conquered territory.
He should give the eastern quarter to the *hotṛ*, the southern to the *brahman* and the *adhvaryu*, and the western and northern to the *udgātṛ*.
Whatever else remains besides the field and the men—this applies to both alternatives.

Or, as long as they might say, "We do not desire more than this," he should give one hundred and forty-eight thousand [cows] to those who perform the central work; twenty-four to each of the half-sharers (*ardhinī*); twelve to each of the third-sharers (*tṛtīyinī*); and six to each of the quarter-sharers (*pādinī*). These are the minimum; however, he may give more at his pleasure.
Its variations are sixteen;
one should arrange these very fifteen *stoma* days [in those ways].

In all *satra* sacrifices, they should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the purchase [of Soma] (*kraya*), the *prasava* [ritual], and the rising (*utthāna*) during the first fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
If one of these cannot be performed, the purchase should take place in the second fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), as should the *prasava*. This applies if two [of the rites] are omitted.
In the three [sacrifices], there should be rising [from the fast] only during the first fortnight;
for them, there are twelve initiation days (dīkṣā) and likewise twelve preparatory days (upasad), unless otherwise specified; and this also applies to those sacrifices lasting a year.
After the consecrations (*dīkṣā*), one may act according to one's desire.
Dhānaṃjayya says that in the first fifteen-night rite there are nineteen consecrations;

Thus ends the first section in the twenty-eighth chapter of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrauta Sūtra. 1. One should chant the *ṣoḍaśin* on the *śakvarī* verses; the *gaurīvita* should be used for the *mahānāmnī* verses. 1.

Because of the various *brahmasāman*s; because of the connection with the *viśvajit*;

During the *upasads* at the *gārhapatya* fire, they should have clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) made into a paste for the purpose of anointing the eyes and anointing the body. Gautama maintains that it should be the Sarvastoma alone; some say it should be the Pṛṣṭhya.

Regarding the Abhiplava [six-day periods], some say that in the [twelve-month] year-long sacrifice, the first Prāyaṇīya [opening day] should be the one belonging to the Daśarātra; others say it should be performed as the Trivṛt [stoma] alone. However, having impelled the Prāyaṇīya, one adopts its modification of the Stomas.
Furthermore, there is no application of individual components for the ten-night [sacrifice].
The teachers maintain that in the *āvṛtta* and *abhiplava* [periods], there should be the *śākvara-varṇa* [chanting] in order to favor the substance of the annual [rite].

They press [the Soma] with a specific intention during the Śatarātra sacrifice. There would be an option regarding whether they press it together or not (16).

Some [perform] the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha];

The months of Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha are optional; likewise Āṣāḍha with the fortnight of Caitra. Or, having been initiated on the sixth day, they should perform seventeen initiations.
By this it is stated that, in the absence of a specific instruction, the annual rites are to be performed annually.
